title: Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment) Bill
what_it_is: Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment) Bill

sections.label: White Paper and Bill Reading
sections.summary: The Government studied the report, presented a White Paper on 15 September 2016, and introduced proposed constitutional amendments at the Bill's First Reading on 10 October 2016.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
sentences.text: The Government studied the report and responded by presenting a White Paper to Parliament on 15 September 2016.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
sentences.text: The proposed constitutional amendments were introduced at the First Reading of the Bill on 10 October 2016.

sections.label: Elected Presidency origins
sections.summary: The Elected Presidency was first conceptualised in the 1980s to guard against the risk of a profligate government squandering the nation's Reserves.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
sentences.text: The Elected Presidency was first conceptualised in the 1980s, to guard against the risk of a profligate government squandering the nation's Reserves.

sections.label: Elected Presidency veto powers
sections.summary: Parliament decided to establish an Elected Presidency with specific veto powers, while the right and responsibility to govern remained with Parliament and the Cabinet.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
sentences.text: Parliament decided that the most effective solution for Singapore was to establish an Elected Presidency with specific veto powers.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
sentences.text: The right and responsibility to govern the country would remain with Parliament and the Cabinet.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
sentences.text: However, he would have additional non-executive custodial powers over two important areas: the spending of past Reserves and key appointments to the public services.

sections.label: Custodial role safeguarding assets
sections.summary: The Elected Presidency plays an important custodial role in safeguarding key assets in a way a purely Parliamentary process cannot.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
sentences.text: The Elected Presidency plays an important custodial role in safeguarding our key assets, in a way a purely Parliamentary process cannot.

sections.label: Reserves use and Commission
sections.summary: The Government sought President SR Nathan's approval to use nearly $5 billion of past Reserves and guarantee about $150 billion of bank deposits, later appointing an independent Constitutional Commission.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
sentences.text: Faced with crippling circumstances, the Government sought the approval of the then-President, the late Mr SR Nathan, to use nearly $5 billion of past Reserves to save businesses and jobs, and to guarantee about $150 billion of bank deposits to keep confidence in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
sentences.text: When our economy recovered, the sum drawn down was returned by the Government to the past Reserves by 2011.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
sentences.text: The Government, therefore, appointed an independent Constitutional Commission earlier this year to review: (a) the qualifying process for Presidential candidacy; (b) the safeguarding of minority representation in the Presidency; and (c) the framework governing the President's custodial powers.

sections.label: White Paper on amendments
sections.summary: After considering the report, the Government presented a White Paper to the House explaining its position and the details of the proposed constitutional amendments.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
sentences.text: After considering the report, the Government presented a White Paper to this House explaining our position and the details of the proposed constitutional amendments which are the subject of this Bill.

sections.label: Eligibility criteria for President updated
sections.summary: Clause 7 amends Article 19 to update eligibility criteria, as GDP, reserves and CPF balances grew and company capital rose.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Our gross domestic product (GDP), Official Foreign Reserves and Central Provident Fund balances have grown by approximately six, seven and eight times, respectively.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: In 1993, there were only 158 companies, or about 0.2% of Singapore-incorporated companies then, which met the $100 million paid-up capital requirement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Today, there is a much larger base of Singapore companies, and the smallest of the top 0.2% has a paid-up capital of approximately $431 million, and if you go back to the 158th largest Singapore-incorporated company today, it has a paid-up capital of approximately S$1.6 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: There is, therefore, a need to update and refine the eligibility criteria.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Clause 7 of the Bill amends Article 19 for this purpose.

sections.label: Twenty-year look-back period
sections.summary: The Bill keeps the three-year tenure and adds a currency period requiring service to fall within the preceding 20 years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: The Bill retains the three-year qualifying tenure, but introduces, in Article 19(2)(g)(ii), a "look-back" or currency period that applies to all qualifying routes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Any period of service a candidate relies on must fall partly or wholly within the 20 years that immediately precede the date of the Writ of Election.

sections.label: Chief executive and Fifth Schedule entities
sections.summary: Article 19(3)(b) narrows qualifying offices to chief executive and expands entities to Fifth Schedule Government companies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: As compared to the existing limb (ii), Article 19(3)(b) narrows the qualifying offices to only the "chief executive" of the Fifth Schedule entity. "Chief executive" is defined in Article 19(10) as "the most senior executive who is principally responsible for the management and conduct of the entity's business and operations".

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Article 19(3)(b) also expands the qualifying entities beyond the Fifth Schedule Statutory Boards to also include Fifth Schedule Government companies, such as GIC Private Limited and Temasek Holdings (Private) Limited.

sections.label: Fifth Schedule threshold raised
sections.summary: Clauses 13(b) and 14(b) raise the qualifying threshold for adding entities to the Fifth Schedule from $100 million to $500 million.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: To ensure that Fifth Schedule entities are of sufficient size, clauses 13(b) and 14(b) of the Bill update the qualifying threshold for adding entities to the Fifth Schedule, from $100 million to $500 million.

sections.label: Shareholders' equity threshold
sections.summary: A company must average at least $500 million shareholders' equity during the person's most recent three-year service as chief executive.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: The company must have, on average, at least $500 million shareholders' equity during the person's most recent three-year period of service as chief executive.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: The updated quantitative threshold of $500 million reflects the vastly different economic climate today, compared to 25 years ago.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: While the increase in the quantitative threshold may sound large, significantly more companies fulfil the updated size requirement today than companies which fulfilled the existing criteria in 1993.

sections.label: Committee and Parliament increase amount
sections.summary: A committee of all PEC members may recommend an increase, which Parliament by resolution may accept fully or partly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: The amount can be increased if a committee, consisting of all PEC members: one, recommends an increase; and two, Parliament, by resolution, either agrees to the full increase or chooses to increase it by less than the recommended amount.

sections.label: President vacates office if not citizen
sections.summary: New Article 22L(1)(aa) provides that a President vacates his office if he ceases to be a citizen of Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: The new Article 22L(1)(aa) provides that a President vacates his office if he ceases to be a citizen of Singapore.

sections.label: Clause 6 repeals Article 18
sections.summary: Clause 6 of the Bill repeals and re-enacts Article 18 to strengthen the PEC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Clause 6 of the Bill repeals and re-enacts Article 18 to strengthen the PEC.

sections.label: PEC additional members and terms
sections.summary: Article 18(2) adds three members to the PEC, and Article 18(3) gives appointed members six-year terms with possible re-appointment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Article 18(2) augments the PEC with three additional members, so as to expand the PEC's expertise to deal with these additional responsibilities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Article 18(2) adds: (a) a past or current CPA member appointed by the CPA Chairman; (b) a person who must be qualified to be, or have been, a Judge of the Supreme Court, appointed by the Chief Justice; and (c) a person who has private sector expertise and experience that is relevant to the functions of the PEC, appointed by the Prime Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Article 18(3) stipulates that appointed PEC members will hold six-year terms and may be re-appointed.

sections.label: Appointment revocation during Presidential election
sections.summary: Article 18(6) specifies an appointment cannot be revoked from the issuance of a Presidential election writ until a person is declared elected.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: This mirrors the existing approach for the PCMR member who sits on the PEC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: However, Article 18(6) specifies that an appointment cannot be revoked from the time a writ for a Presidential election is issued to the time a person is declared to be elected as President.

sections.label: Constitutional Commission five-term hiatus model
sections.summary: After considering many models, the Constitutional Commission recommended a five-term hiatus model, which the Government accepted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: After considering many different models, the Constitutional Commission recommended a "five-term hiatus" model, which the Government has accepted.

sections.label: Reserved election for racial group
sections.summary: Article 19B(1) reserves the next election for a racial group that has not held the Presidency for five consecutive terms, unless no eligible candidate comes forward.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Elections will generally be open to candidates from all races.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: However, if a particular racial group has not held the Presidency for the most recent five consecutive terms, Article 19B(1) reserves the next election for candidates from that group.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: If, during a reserved election, no eligible candidate from the relevant racial group comes forward, the election becomes an open election.

sections.label: Racial groups for reserved elections
sections.summary: Article 19B(6) defines three racial groups for reserved elections: Chinese, Malay, and a composite Indian and other minority group.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Article 19B(6) defines the three racial groups that reserved elections can apply to: (a) the Chinese community; (b) the Malay community; and (c) a composite group comprising the Indian community and other minority communities in Singapore.

sections.label: Chinese community candidate definition
sections.summary: A similar definition will determine whether a Presidential candidate is Chinese, requiring self-identification and general acceptance by the community.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: A similar definition will be introduced for the purposes of determining whether a Presidential candidate belongs to the Chinese community.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: These racial community definitions have two aspects – an applicant must consider himself a member of the relevant community, and must also be generally accepted by that community as a member.

sections.label: Bill's five framework changes
sections.summary: The Bill changes five areas: President's CPA consultation, Parliamentary overruling, veto time limits, disclosure of reasons, and strengthening the CPA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: The Bill improves the framework by making changes to the following areas: (a) first, the President's obligation to consult the CPA; (b) second, the Parliamentary overruling framework; (c) third, time limits for the exercise of President's veto; (d) fourth, disclosure of the President's and CPA's reasons; and (e) fifth, strengthening the CPA.

sections.label: Overruling extended to fiscal matters
sections.summary: New Article 37IF provisions extend the overruling mechanism uniformly to all fiscal and appointment-related matters subject to a Presidential veto.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: The new Article 37IF(1), (2)(a) and (c), and (3) extends the overruling mechanism uniformly to all fiscal and appointment-related matters subject to a Presidential veto.

sections.label: Veto time limits and urgency
sections.summary: Article 21A sets a 30-day limit for specified matters, six weeks for others, and allows reduction to a minimum 15 days if urgent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Article 21A(2)(a) provides that a 30-day time limit applies for certain time-sensitive matters, namely: (i) Supply Bills, Supplementary Supply Bills and Final Supply Bills; (ii) the President's additional protective functions relating to ISA detentions, MRHA restraining orders and CPIB investigations; and (iii) amendments relating to entrenched provisions, when the entrenchment framework is brought into operation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: For all other matters, Article 21A(2)(b) imposes a six-week time limit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Article 21A(3)(a) provides that where the Prime Minister certifies that a matter is urgent, the default time limit can be reduced to a minimum of 15 days.

sections.label: CPA recommendation deadlines
sections.summary: The CPA must recommend within 15 days under a 30-day limit, or within three weeks under a six-week limit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: If the President has a 30-day time limit, the CPA must make its recommendation within 15 days.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: If the President has a six-week time limit, the CPA must make its recommendation within three weeks.

sections.label: CPA recommendation deadline
sections.summary: The CPA must recommend at least five days before the President's deadline, or it is deemed to have recommended against a veto.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: In all cases, notwithstanding any extensions granted, the CPA must give its recommendation at least five days before the President's time limit for signifying his decision.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: If the CPA fails to give its recommendation within the stipulated time limit, it is deemed by Article 37IC(4) to have recommended against the exercise of a Presidential veto.

sections.label: CPA eight members
sections.summary: The CPA will have eight members: three appointed by the President, three on the Prime Minister's advice, and one each on the Chief Justice's and PSC Chairman's advice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: The CPA will, therefore, have eight members in all: three appointed by the President in his own discretion; three appointed on the advice of the Prime Minister; and one each appointed on the advice of the Chief Justice and the PSC Chairman.

sections.label: CPA division appointments
sections.summary: Each division has one member appointed by the President and one on the Prime Minister's advice, with the first division also having a Chief Justice appointee and the second a PSC Chairman appointee.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Each division has one member appointed by the President in his discretion and one member appointed on the Prime Minister's advice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: In addition, the first division has a member appointed on the Chief Justice's advice, and the second division has a member appointed on the PSC Chairman's advice.

sections.label: Appointee criteria and entrenchment
sections.summary: Clause 19 inserts Article 37D(2) requiring appointing authorities to consider a potential appointee's integrity, character, reputation, and relevant expertise and experience.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Third, clause 19 of the Bill inserts a new Article 37D(2) that requires appointing authorities to consider whether a potential appointee (a) is of integrity, good character and reputation; and (b) has expertise and experience relevant to the matters on which the CPA may have to advise the President on.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: The entrenchment framework introduces additional safeguards, over and above the existing requirement of a two-third Parliamentary majority for constitutional amendments, to further entrench certain specific constitutional provisions.

sections.label: Commission on entrenchment framework
sections.summary: The Constitutional Commission observed that the entrenchment framework, if brought into force, makes amending entrenched provisions virtually impossible.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: As the Constitutional Commission observed, the entrenchment framework – if brought into force – renders it "virtually impossible" to amend any aspect of the entrenched provisions.

sections.label: Streamlining entrenchment framework
sections.summary: The entrenchment framework will be streamlined to cover only provisions establishing the Elected Presidency and its core custodial powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: There is a risk that a government bent on raiding the Reserves or compromising the Public Services could remove the Elected Presidency to get rid of that check.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: This was the initial rationale for entrenchment: to protect the Elected Presidency and its core custodial powers against easy removal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: By contrast, it would be much more difficult to remove well-established institutions, such as this Parliament or the Judiciary.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: We will, therefore, streamline the entrenchment framework to cover only the provisions establishing the Elected Presidency and its core custodial powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Other provisions which do not relate to these areas will remain protected in the same way as the rest of the Constitution, that is, through the need for a two-third majority in Parliament to amend these provisions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: The second consideration is whether the referendum requirement should be revised.

sections.label: Circumspect use of referendums
sections.summary: Referendums should be used in a circumspect way.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Referendums should, therefore, be used in a circumspect way.

sections.label: Bill replaces framework with tiers
sections.summary: The Bill replaces this framework with one that categorises the entrenched provisions into two tiers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: The Bill replaces this framework with one that categorises the entrenched provisions into two tiers.

sections.label: Referendum threshold revised
sections.summary: The referendum threshold is revised from a two-third majority to a simple majority, with two-thirds reserved for sovereignty and forces provisions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: The required referendum threshold will also be revised from a two-third majority to a simple majority.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: A two-third referendum majority requirement should thus be reserved only for provisions relating to the surrender of Singapore's sovereignty and relinquishment of our Police and Armed Forces, or amendments to those provisions, as currently already provided under our Constitution.

sections.label: Introduction and passage requirements
sections.summary: A Bill may be introduced where the President concurs or withholds concurrence contrary to the CPA's recommendation, or is supported by a simple majority at a referendum, and must still be passed by a two-third Parliamentary majority.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: First, where the President concurs with the introduction of the Bill, or the President withholds concurrence contrary to the CPA's recommendation; or second, where the Bill is supported by a simple majority at a national referendum.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Under Article 5A(5), regardless of how the Bill is introduced, the Bill must still subsequently be passed by a two-third Parliamentary majority.

sections.label: Article 5B Bills
sections.summary: A Bill under Article 5B may be introduced ordinarily but passed only by a three-quarter Parliamentary majority, and the President may withhold assent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: A Bill to which Article 5B applies may be introduced in the ordinary way like other constitutional amendment Bills.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: However, it can subsequently be passed only by a three-quarter Parliamentary majority.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Under Article 5C(1), the President may withhold assent to such a Bill.

sections.label: Overruling withheld assent
sections.summary: Where the President withholds assent with CPA's support, he may be overruled by a simple majority at a referendum or a three-quarter Parliamentary majority affirming the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Where he withholds assent with CPA's support, he may be overruled if the Bill is supported by a simple majority at a referendum, or a three-quarter Parliamentary majority affirms the Bill.

sections.label: NCMPs number and voting rights
sections.summary: Clause 25 amends Article 39 to raise the maximum number of NCMPs from nine to 12 and give them the same voting rights as Members of Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: Clause 25 of the Bill, therefore, amends Article 39 to increase the maximum number of NCMPs from nine to 12, and to give them the same voting rights as Members of Parliament.

sections.label: Five-term hiatus for Presidency
sections.summary: The proposed five-term hiatus mechanism helps, where necessary, facilitate the periodic election of members of different racial groups to the Presidency.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: The proposed five-term hiatus mechanism helps, where necessary, to facilitate the periodic election of members of different racial groups to the Presidency.

sections.label: Improving Elected Presidency custodial powers
sections.summary: These add to efforts to improve the Elected Presidency so custodial powers are exercised timely, with weight given to CPA advice, providing stability and avoiding gridlock.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: These add to our continuing efforts to improve the Elected Presidency so that the President's custodial powers are exercised in a timely manner, and with sufficient weight given to the collective advice of the CPA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: This will provide stability to our system and also help to avoid gridlock in situations where the President and the Government do not agree.

sections.label: Presidency as symbol and ballast
sections.summary: The amendments seek to enhance the Presidency's ability to remain a symbol Singaporeans identify with and to safeguard Reserves and key appointments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: We want to make sure that the Presidency remains a symbol Singaporeans from all communities will continue to identify with.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: But since 1991, it has also become an important part of our ballast system, stabilising our ship by safeguarding the two key areas – our Reserves and key appointments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
sentences.text: The proposed amendments seek to enhance the ability of the Presidency to play both these important roles, to help keep our people united and our country stable.

sections.label: Two key components of Bill
sections.summary: Two key components of the Bill stand out, and an Elected Presidency with reserve powers to safeguard Reserves was introduced in 1991.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: When studying the amendments set out in this Bill, there are two key components that stand out to me and which I would like to talk about in this debate.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: We had introduced in 1991 an Elected Presidency with reserve powers to safeguard our Reserves.

sections.label: President's custodial role and mandate
sections.summary: The President's custodial role is to safeguard Reserves if the Government goes rogue, and without an electoral mandate it would be almost impossible to challenge the Government.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: First and foremost, and the most important, the custodial role of the President is to safeguard our Reserves should the Government of the day go rogue and, hence, the metaphor of the President as holding a "second key".

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: And because the Government of the day is formed by the Party that had won Singaporeans' mandate, it would be almost impossible for the President to challenge the Government if the President has no electoral mandate to back him.

sections.label: Support for Elected President
sections.summary: The speaker supports an Elected President with moral authority to safeguard Singapore's Reserves against a rogue government.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: With the enhanced eligibility criteria, I believe the qualifying candidates will not have such an issue.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Therefore, I am supportive of having an Elected President because he or she must have the moral authority to stand against a government that has gone rogue.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: He or she must be able to safeguard our Reserves, which are sacrosanct to Singapore's long-term survival as an economy and as a nation.

sections.label: Company equity and racial prejudice
sections.summary: Under updated criteria, far less than 1% of registered companies have $500 million shareholder equity, and a 2014 study found racial prejudice persists.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Under the updated criteria, far less than 1% of the total number of registered companies in Singapore will have shareholder equity of $500 million.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: The IPS Study on Race and Religion in Singapore by Dr Matthew Matthews released in 2014 revealed that racial prejudice continues to be present in modern Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: And 62.8% of respondents think there is about the same or more racial prejudice in Singapore today compared to five years ago.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Non-Chinese are four times more likely to feel racially discriminated against regarding a job or job promotion, compared to Chinese.

sections.label: Increase in qualified companies
sections.summary: Qualified companies under the same criteria have increased to more than 2,000, over ten times as many.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Today, qualified companies based on the same criteria have increased to more than 2,000, more than 10 times as many.

sections.label: Raising qualifying criteria
sections.summary: The speaker says the situation will lead to more problems than benefits, so qualifying criteria must be raised for competent candidates.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Such a situation will definitely lead to more problems than benefits.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Hence, it is necessary to raise the qualifying criteria to make sure that every candidate is competent.

sections.label: Meritocracy and reserved election
sections.summary: The speaker believes meritocracy and multiracialism are equally important, and reserved election candidates must meet the same stringent qualifying criteria.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Some people are concerned that a hiatus-triggered reserve election will weaken meritocracy, an equally important founding principle.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: I believe that meritocracy and multiracialism are equally important and a reserved election does not mean that we have to compromise one or the other.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Be it normal Presidential election or reserved election, all the candidates must meet the same stringent qualifying criteria.

sections.label: Majority race supporting Bill
sections.summary: The speaker says the majority race should act on its belief in multiracialism and support this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: If we sincerely believe in the value of multiracialism, we, as the majority race, should take our stand and act upon what we believe to support this Bill.

sections.label: Nation-founding philosophy and qualifying criteria
sections.summary: The speaker says Singapore must keep working hard with the same nation-founding philosophy and agrees the qualifying criteria should change so candidates can manage financial resources.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Hence, we must continue to work hard and forge ahead with the same nation-founding philosophy.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: I agree on the need to change the qualifying criteria so that the potential candidate has the experience to deal with how our sizeable financial resources should be managed.

sections.label: Circuit breaker for minority president
sections.summary: The passage says the circuit breaker, described euphemistically, is a tweak guaranteeing a minority person a chance to become Elected President.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: While being presented euphemistically as a circuit breaker in successive elections of the Elected President, it is a tweak that guarantees a chance for a person from the minority to become the Elected President.

sections.label: Surveys on race and president
sections.summary: A CNA-IPS study found most Singaporeans prefer a president of their own race, and an MCI survey found most agreed to a minority president but baulked at the circuit breaker.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: The recent study by CNA-IPS found that, given a choice, most Singaporeans prefer someone of the same race as President.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: More than 80% of respondents of Malays and Indians said that they would accept a Singaporean Chinese as President.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: However, less than 70% of Chinese respondents found a Singaporean Malay or Indian to be acceptable as President.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Furthermore, according to a Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) survey, when asked if they think we should have a minority as an Elected President, the vast majority, including the Chinese, agreed wholeheartedly.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: However, when presented with the circuit breaker option, the majority baulked.

sections.label: Older Malays and Malay president
sections.summary: The passage says older Malays who lived under a Malay president understandably yearn for one, and Singapore has had no Malay president for 46 years since Yusof Ishak died in 1970.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Among the older Malays, having lived under a Malay president, it is understandable that they yearn for one after a very long time.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: We have not had a Malay president for 46 years.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Our first President, the late Mr Yusof Ishak died in office on 23 November 1970.

sections.label: Few Malays in power
sections.summary: The passage states that Singapore does not have many Malays in key positions of power and leadership.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: The truth is that we do not have many Malays in key positions of power and leadership.

sections.label: Quality of candidates and president roles
sections.summary: The speaker's final point concerns the quality of candidates, noting the Elected President has two equally important roles, ceremonial and custodial.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: I now come to my final point, which is about the quality of the candidates.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: There are two equally important roles of the Elected President – ceremonial and custodial.

sections.label: Elected Presidency minority chance
sections.summary: Proposed Elected Presidency changes aim to give minority communities a chance to become President, supported by CNA-IPS and MCI study findings.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: The changes proposed to the Elected Presidency will ensure the minority communities will have the chance to become an Elected President.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: The results of a study by CNA-IPS show that, if given the opportunity, a large majority of Singaporeans will tend to choose a candidate from their own community as President.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Meanwhile, an MCI study showed that, when asked whether Singapore needs a minority as an Elected President, the majority of respondents, including Chinese respondents, agreed.

sections.label: Malay candidate support concern
sections.summary: The speaker worries a Malay candidate may lack full support and says strict criteria should not change for minority representation alone.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: I am concerned that the Malay candidate will not have the full support of other Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: So, I firmly state that we should not change the strict criteria that was established.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: If the change is done to ensure a minority representation, it must be done because it is good for Singapore and all Singaporeans, and not just for the minority groups.

sections.label: Enhancements to Elected Presidency framework
sections.summary: The speaker supports proposed enhancements to the Elected Presidency framework to ensure the best qualified person is elected.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: We want a president to command the respect of all Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
sentences.text: I, therefore, stand by the proposed enhancements to the Elected Presidency framework because, first and foremost, these enhancements serve to ensure that the best qualified person who reflects the values and ethos of our nation will be elected to the highest office of our land.

sections.label: Minority deputies in French Assembly
sections.summary: A 2009 New York Times study reported only three of 555 French National Assembly deputies were from minority backgrounds.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Yet, the New York Times reported in a 2009 study that of the 555 deputies elected to the National Assembly in metropolitan France, just three – three out of 555 – were from minority backgrounds.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: To put this in perspective, depending on which study you look at, between 10% and 20% of the French people have foreign origins, represented that year by three out of more than 500 deputies in the French National Assembly.

sections.label: Reserved elections as safety valve
sections.summary: Reserved elections are described as a safety valve so every generation can see a President from its own community.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Candidates face the same finish line, but some will have had to walk further, longer and harder just to get to the starting line.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: They were controversial at the beginning but, today, we see their value as a safety check, to avoid a freak election result where every elected Member of Parliament is of the majority race.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Likewise, there is value in having reserved elections as a safety valve for the Elected Presidency, so that every generation has a chance to see a President elected from their own community.

sections.label: Strengthening multiracialism together
sections.summary: The passage says Singaporeans can strengthen multiracialism so reserved election provisions may someday never need to be triggered.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: It bends when all of us, Singaporeans from all walks of life, put our hands upon it, and move as one.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: We all can play a part to strengthen our multiracialism, so that someday, these provisions of a reserved election will never need to be triggered, when we have become a more perfectly united people.

sections.label: Racial harmony everyone's responsibility
sections.summary: Maintaining racial harmony is everyone's responsibility, not just the Government's or national leaders'.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Maintaining racial harmony is not just the responsibility of the Government or national leaders, it is everyone's responsibility, too.

sections.label: Learning other communities' languages cultures
sections.summary: Children should learn other communities' languages and cultures through communication and interaction, as mutual understanding strengthens social cohesion.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: In Singapore, we promote the importance of mother tongue from young.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Likewise, we should encourage our children to – through communication and interaction – learn about other communities' languages and cultures.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: This is because mutual understanding can overcome gaps and deepen understanding, thereby strengthening our nation's social cohesion.

sections.label: Reserved election for minority communities
sections.summary: The responsibility for multiracialism now falls on this generation, and proposed Article 19B provides for a reserved election for a community.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: This never-ending mission was once the work of our Pioneers, our Pioneer Generation Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: That responsibility now falls on us, our generation of Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: It is up to all of us to live the values of multiracialism, to live those values as best we can in what we do.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: It is up to all of us to try and build a better Singapore for our children and grandchildren, regardless of race, language or religion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In my speech, I will focus on the proposed Article 19B which provides for a reserved election for a community that has not held the office of the President for five or more consecutive terms.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In effect, this provision, if passed, would ensure that the office of the President, from time to time, would be held by persons drawn from the minority communities.

sections.label: Article 152 Malay community interests
sections.summary: Article 152 of the Constitution gives the Government responsibility to care for racial and religious minorities, particularly the Malay community.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: But the Malay community placed full trust and worked with the Government which, on its part, also ensured that the community's interests are always protected, in recognition of their commitment to the country.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This may be a good time to remind ourselves that this is why Article 152 of our Constitution was enacted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It is provided in our Constitution that the Government has a responsibility to constantly care for the interests of the racial and religious minorities in Singapore and, in particular, those of the Malay community as the indigenous people of Singapore.

sections.label: Viewing proposed Article 19B
sections.summary: These issues have been handled constructively, but this cannot be taken for granted, and proposed Article 19B should be viewed against this background.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Whilst, thus far, these issues have been dealt with constructively and responsibly and against the broader context of ensuring that our communities progress as a whole, we cannot take for granted that this will always be the case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It is against this background that we should view the proposed Article 19B.

sections.label: Malay community meritocratic multiracial ideals
sections.summary: This is as important as the Malay community's 1965 commitment to meritocratic and multiracial ideals, without encouraging voting on racial lines.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This is, in my view, as important an overture as the decision on the part of the Malay community in August 1965 to be fully subscribed to the meritocratic and multiracial ideals of an emerging Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This does not mean that the Singapore electorate is, therefore, being encouraged to vote on racial lines for the Elected President on the basis that there is a guarantee of a minority candidate being fielded from time to time.

sections.label: Minority President inclusion provision
sections.summary: If 30 years pass without a minority-community President, the inclusion provision will kick in to keep society inclusive.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Should, however, there be a situation where 30 years have elapsed without a President drawn from the minority community, then, for the sake of ensuring we always remain an inclusive society, the inclusion provision will kick in.

sections.label: Article 19B minority President
sections.summary: Article 19B ensures a minority-community member becomes President from time to time, weaving inclusiveness into Singapore's constitutional DNA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: With Article 19B, we ensure that we will have a member of the minority community becoming the President of Singapore, the highest office in the land, from time to time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: With this, we will not lose our perspectives as we face and manage difficult and sensitive issues like the tudung.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, Article 19B really strikes at what it means to be a Singaporean.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It weaves into our constitutional DNA that all Singaporeans now and generations to come, regardless of race, are part of and are important to the Singapore story founded on inclusiveness.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Since the Opening of Parliament in January, we have had a full programme.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: We have implemented Silver Support and MediShield Life; we have expanded SkillsFuture; we have been busy building our infrastructure, housing and transport.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: It is good politics that enables Singapore to have a Government that produces good policies, one that is responsible and does the right thing; serves the people; safeguards our stability and success; leads the country to greater heights.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: That is why in January, I raised the subject of the Elected President and then appointed a Constitutional Commission to review the Elected Presidency scheme.

sections.label: Constitutional Commission report and White Paper
sections.summary: The Constitutional Commission received over 100 public submissions, held two months of hearings, and published its report; the Government then published a White Paper.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: The Constitutional Commission received over 100 submissions from the public, held two months of public hearings, deliberated and published their report two months ago.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: In September, the Government published a White Paper setting out the changes that we would make.

sections.label: DPM Teo explains Bill
sections.summary: Yesterday, Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean spent 90 minutes explaining the Bill.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Yesterday, Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean spent 90 minutes explaining the Bill.

sections.label: Elected President history and working
sections.summary: Mr Lee proposed an Elected President in 1984, it was legislated in 1990, and the scheme has worked well for a quarter of a century.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: That is how important maintaining the integrity of the Public Service was to our founding generational leaders.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: So, after 20 years with the Reserves to worry about, with the Civil Service and the high quality, Mr Lee proposed the idea in 1984 of an Elected President.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: And the idea was debated, refined and eventually legislated in 1990.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: For the past quarter of a century since we have implemented the scheme, the Elected Presidency has worked well and become a valuable part of our political system.

sections.label: Candidate's $60 billion economic plan
sections.summary: One candidate championed a $60 billion economic plan, supposedly to create jobs and enterprise.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: One candidate championed a $60 billion economic plan, supposedly to create jobs and enterprise.

sections.label: Elected President as a plus
sections.summary: The speaker says some 2011 candidates put election before the Constitution, but calls the Elected President a plus for the system.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: But in 2011, some candidates' attitude was: never mind, just say it, get elected first, worry about the Constitution later on.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: But for all these difficulties, I am convinced that the Elected President has been a plus for our system.

sections.label: Ceremonial President, CPA power
sections.summary: A suggestion is to revert to a ceremonial President chosen by Parliament and give the second key to the CPA.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: The second suggestion is to revert to a ceremonial President chosen by Parliament, not elected in a national election, but vest the second key in the Council of Presidential Advisers (CPA), give the power to the CPA.

sections.label: Parliament supreme, President's influence
sections.summary: The speaker says let Parliament be supreme, and that the Elected President's powers have influenced Singapore politics for the better.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Let Parliament be supreme, with unrestricted power to do as it pleases.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: I believe that over the last 25 years, even though the Elected President has never had to veto any spending proposal by the Government, by the very existence of his powers, he has influenced Singapore politics for the better.

sections.label: Boom revenue saved and spent
sections.summary: A report concluded that during the boom, of every AUD19 in extra revenue, the government saved AUD1 and spent AUD18.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Somebody subsequently did a report which concluded that during the boom, out of every AUD19 that the government received in additional revenue, it saved AUD1 and it spent AUD18.

sections.label: Second key held by Elected President
sections.summary: MPs answered that spending need not be worried about as a good investment, so the second key should be held by the Elected President.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: In fact, on the contrary, when spending proposals come up and we pressed the Members of Parliament (MPs), "How are they to be paid for?" The answer is, "You don't have to worry.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: This is a good investment." And that is why we need the second key to be held by another elected institution, separate from Parliament, and that is the Elected President.

sections.label: Second key, independent institution
sections.summary: The second key would be held by the Elected President, a different and independent institution elected separately with a different term.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: What the Chinese call, "孤注一掷" (gu zhu yi zhi), that Page: 35 is, put all your chips there and risk it.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: That is why we decided that, in Singapore, the second key would be held by the Elected President, a different and independent institution, elected in a separate Presidential Election with a different term of office from the Government.

sections.label: Elected President as safeguard
sections.summary: The Elected President was introduced as a safeguard to protect Reserves and appointments and address Singapore's specific vulnerabilities.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: We started very close to the first extreme ‒ a unicameral, single Parliament, untrammelled.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: We introduced this safeguard, the Elected President, to protect Reserves and appointments, and address specific vulnerabilities which we have in Singapore.

sections.label: Elected President as stabiliser
sections.summary: Besides elected Parliament as primary control, the Elected President serves as a stabiliser, and its role should be kept and finetuned.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: You need other ideas to make a complete and a stable system.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: I do not think the system like the US can work for Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: But we, too, need some "auxiliary precautions", some stabiliser, besides the "primary control", which is the fact that Parliament is elected by the people.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: And for us, that stabiliser is the Elected President.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Therefore, we should keep the Elected President and finetune its stabiliser role.

sections.label: Multiracial symbol of Presidency
sections.summary: A President always from one race would not credibly symbolise the multiracial nation; every community should know one of its own can become President.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: If the President, who is a symbol of a multiracial nation, always comes from the same race, not only will he cease to be a credible symbol of our nation, the very multiracial character of our nation will come under question.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Every citizen – Chinese, Malay, Indian, or some other race – should know that someone of his community can become President and, in fact, from time to time, does become Page: 37 President.

sections.label: Singapore as multiracial Southeast Asian country
sections.summary: Forgetting that Singapore is independent, sovereign, multiracial and in Southeast Asia can cause misunderstandings and unrealistic expectations; it is not a Chinese country.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: It can lead to misunderstandings; it can lead to unrealistic expectations; it can lead to us being carried away even domestically and forgetting this fundamental fact about Singapore – that we are independent, sovereign, multiracial, in Southeast Asia.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: And that is what we must always remember: we are not a Chinese country.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: We are a multiracial, multi-religious Southeast Asian country with an ethnic Chinese majority but not a Chinese country.

sections.label: External terrorist attack response
sections.summary: A terrorist attack is frightening, but if it comes from outside it is not so hard to understand and people pull together.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: A terrorist attack is frightening but if it comes from outside, I think it is not so hard to understand; we pull together.

sections.label: Presidency must be multiracial
sections.summary: Singaporeans look up to the President as personifying what Singapore stands for, so the Presidency must be multiracial.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Singaporeans look up to the President as the personification of all that Singapore stands for and all that we stand for in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: So, it is a fundamental necessity that the Presidency be multiracial.

sections.label: Multiracial Presidency election arrangements
sections.summary: The office will be de-facto multiracial without formal constitutional arrangements, but without deliberate arrangements the Presidency could become single-race over time.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: And the office will, de-facto, be multiracial, without explicit, formal constitutional arrangements.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: But if the President is elected in a national election, then if we do not make deliberate arrangements to ensure a multiracial outcome, the Presidency could well, over time, become a single-race office, because minorities do find it harder to win in a national election.

sections.label: Hiatus-triggered reserved election model
sections.summary: Arrangements are made now to ensure a multiracial Presidency through a hiatus-triggered model reserving a term after five consecutive terms without a President from a community.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: So, the moral of the story is that race and religion are very deep-seated realities in every country.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: So, even though there is no pressure, even the minority communities have not pressed for it in Singapore, we should make arrangements now to ensure that the Presidency will be multiracial.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: We have decided to do this through what the Constitutional Commission has called the hiatus-triggered model, which means that Presidential Elections are generally open to candidates of all races.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: But if we have not had a President from a particular community for five consecutive terms, then the next term will be reserved for candidates from that community.

sections.label: Legislating Presidential Elections Act amendment
sections.summary: The Government intends to legislate when amending the Presidential Elections Act in January next year, counting from Dr Wee Kim Wee.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: The Government intends to legislate when we amend the Presidential Elections Act in January next year.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: We will start counting from the first President who exercised the powers of the Elected President, in other words, Dr Wee Kim Wee.

sections.label: Deeming Presidents' races for reserved election
sections.summary: The Act will deem Dr Wee Kim Wee, Mr Ong Teng Cheong and Dr Tony Tan as Chinese and Mr S R Nathan as Indian, making the next election reserved for Malay candidates.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: There is no practical doubt, but as a legal matter, we have to define it because you cannot convene the Committee retrospectively to certify them.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: So, the Act will deem: (a) Dr Wee Kim Wee as Chinese, (b) Mr Ong Teng Cheong as Chinese, (c) Mr S R Nathan, who served two terms, as Indian, (d) and Dr Tony Tan as Chinese.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Therefore, by the operation of the hiatus-triggered model, the next election, due next year, will be a reserved election for Malay candidates.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: As Minister Yaacob Ibrahim observed yesterday, this would be our first Malay President after more than 46 years, since our first President Encik Yusof Ishak.

sections.label: Tweaking system to stabilise Parliament
sections.summary: The system was tweaked to stabilise the Parliament without changing the fundamental nature of the system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: It is something which we considered carefully and the issue is this.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: We have tweaked the system to stabilise the Parliament but without changing the fundamental nature of this system.

sections.label: Rejecting two-House Parliament
sections.summary: Singapore is too small and lacks the range of people and talent to form two Houses with an Upper House vetting legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: And then I have Parliament making legislation and Upper House vetting, approving legislation, having some powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: We decided, when we went into this, and I think rightly, that Singapore is too small and does not really have the range of people and talent to form two Houses like that.

sections.label: Elected person decides with advisors
sections.summary: The check should be instituted in a well-advised person, with advisors giving inputs but the elected person deciding.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: We are looking for this check to be instituted in a person who is well-advised.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: And we want the person who is elected to make the decision, and the advisors to give him inputs but the elected person decides.

sections.label: Advisors for difficult decisions
sections.summary: Such people may not win elections or rouse crowds but are sought for advice on difficult decisions, an arrangement the President and CPA found prudent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: They may not be people who can easily make a campaign speech and win elections and rouse the crowd, but they are people you will go to for advice when you need to make a difficult decision.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: I have discussed this with the President, he has discussed it with the CPA, and they have found this arrangement to be a prudent and a judicious one.

sections.label: Preventing future government curtailing GE
sections.summary: The question asks what in the system prevents a future government from abolishing or curtailing a GE, noting the Elected Presidency's repeated constitutional amendments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: So, my question to the Prime Minister would be, what within our system would prevent a future government – I do not think the current Government would do that and previous Governments clearly did not – but what in our system will prevent a future government from either abolishing or radically curtailing a GE at some point in the future?

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: So, in Singapore we have to amend the Constitution to do that.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Elected Presidency was created in the 1990s with the intention of safeguarding our past Reserves from being squandered by a "rogue government".

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, the experience with the Elected Presidency has seen the PAP Government coming back to the House to amend the Constitution again and again, as unintended consequences arose.

sections.label: Reserves safeguarded by elected entity
sections.summary: The country's past Reserves should be preserved and strongly safeguarded by an entity elected by the people.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Third, that the country's past Reserves should be preserved and strongly safeguarded by an entity that is elected by the people.

sections.label: Eligibility criteria and pro-PAP President
sections.summary: Under the PAP Government's scheme, strict and specific eligibility criteria would likely see the election of a pro-PAP President.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Under the scheme designed by the PAP Government, the strict and specific eligibility criteria would likely see the election of a pro-PAP President.

sections.label: Head of State versus custodian roles
sections.summary: The Commission noted the Head of State was a unifying role while custodian was confrontational, and an election made the President a partisan figure.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Commission noted that being a Head of State was a unifying role while being a custodian was a confrontational role; in addition, requiring the President to go through an election necessarily made him a partisan figure.

sections.label: WP proposes second Chamber Senate
sections.summary: The WP proposes creating a second Legislative Chamber, a Senate, to safeguard the country's past Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Having considered the Commission's report, the WP believes it is apt to consider creating a second Chamber in the Legislature, which could be called the Senate.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Its primary role would be to safeguard the country's past Reserves.

sections.label: Senate to hold President's powers
sections.summary: The WP proposes vesting the Elected President's discretionary powers in a nationally elected Senate rather than an appointed one.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: To ease the transition from the Elected Presidency system, we propose that all the discretionary powers currently vested in the Elected President be vested in the newly-created Senate.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Under this proposal, the Senate would be elected by the people in a national election, rather than appointed as suggested by the Commission.

sections.label: Articles 5A and 5B
sections.summary: Proposed Articles 5A and 5B let a Bill affecting the President's powers be presented without his agreement or a referendum if the CPA agrees.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The proposed Articles 5A and 5B will enable a Bill affecting the President's role or powers to be presented even if Page: 46 he does not agree and the proposal is not put to a referendum, so long as the CPA agrees to it.

sections.label: Option A, Option B, election timing
sections.summary: The WP prefers Option B, an appointed President without custodial role, and asks why the Government is rushing the matter.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: Option A, as advanced by the PAP Government, is where the President is elected and plays dual roles.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: Option B, which is the model that the WP prefers, is an appointed President without the custodial role which is now vested in an elected Senate.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: Many Singaporeans, including our residents, have asked why the Government is rushing such an important matter through Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: They noted that Prime Minister Lee had said that there was no urgency, while the Law Minister has gone on record that the changes were not targeted at disbarring any individual from running.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: If that is the case, surely, there is still time for any change to be carefully considered for implementation in the following Presidential Election in 2023, rather than the one next year.

sections.label: Public post on Head of State
sections.summary: A member of the public asked what legacy is left when the Head of State is defined by wealth and race.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: The post from a member of the public read as follows, and I quote, "What kind of legacy are we leaving to the next generation when we define our Head of State by his wealth and race, rather than by his character, social contributions and public spiritedness?" Madam, this is, indeed, an important question for all of us to answer.

sections.label: Overemphasis on financial criteria
sections.summary: The speaker says overemphasis on the custodial role and tighter criteria narrows what qualities a President ought to have.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The constant emphasis on the custodial role of the President seems to be the financial acumen and executive experience of the candidate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I agree that times have changed and while the role of the second key to the Reserves is important, but an overemphasis on this in this Bill, manifesting in the tighter criteria of having led a $500-million company to justify the complexity of the role, immediately narrows the consideration of what qualities a President ought to have.

sections.label: Presidential qualification criteria debate
sections.summary: A speaker asks whether the $100 million criteria could have been retained instead of $500 million, and says the three-year profitability criterion does not reflect market reality.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Page: 48 Given the strengthened council that the President can seek wisdom from and the role of Parliament in intervening in a gridlock, could we have then retained the qualification criteria of $100 million in an executive responsibility, instead of $500 million?

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The other criterion under Article 19(4)(a) that the company run by the candidate chief executive officer (CEO) must be profitable over the three-year period does not reflect market reality.

sections.label: Softer criteria for President
sections.summary: A speaker argues for incremental increases to financial criteria and suggests adding softer criteria such as key roles in charities or non-profit organisations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: He is applying to be the President of Singapore, a role that demands a track record of service to society, of demonstrated ability and willingness to have contributed to society and Singaporeans, in a leading role, in addition to his role as custodian of Singapore's Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Therefore, I would argue that perhaps, we could have done the incremental increase for the financial criteria, rather than by a single step.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Complement that criterion with some softer and relevant criteria like maybe the candidate should have played a key role in an organisation that has contributed back to society, say, a charity, community organisation or non-profit organisation.

sections.label: Reserved Presidential Election announcement
sections.summary: A speaker is heartened by the Prime Minister's announcement of a reserved Presidential Election and says many in the Malay community would also be heartened.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Page: 49 I am heartened that the Prime Minister has just announced that the next election would be a reserved Presidential Election and I think many in the Malay community would also be heartened to have potentially a first Malay Elected President for Singapore.

sections.label: Reserved election for minority race
sections.summary: A speaker says the Malay community welcomed a minority provision and welcomes the Constitutional Commission's proposal for a reserved election if no candidate of a race has been elected for over five terms.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: When I touched on this issue in Parliament at that time, I said that the move to have a provision for minorities is welcomed by the Malay community.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I welcome the proposal by the Constitutional Commission that proposed a reserved election for the candidate of a certain race if, for over five terms, no candidate from that race has been elected as President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The Government has also accepted the proposal in its White Paper.

sections.label: Eligibility criteria and meritocracy
sections.summary: A speaker says the concern is understandable because meritocracy is important, and feels the Commission's emphasis on eligibility guarantees any elected candidate must fulfil the set criteria.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: This concern is understandable because meritocracy is an important value in the lives and success of Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: So, I feel that the emphasis by the Commission regarding the level of eligibility is a guarantee that no matter which candidate is elected, he or she must fulfil the criteria that have been set.

sections.label: Multiracialism and veto framework changes
sections.summary: A speaker calls the Prime Minister's proposal courageous given political risk, says the Malay community will welcome it, and says the veto and entrenchment changes strengthen governance and safeguard the Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The Prime Minister's decision to propose this change is a courageous decision, especially in terms of the political risk in convincing the majority community that it needs to be done in order to preserve this principle of multiracialism.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I am certain that this development will be welcomed by the Malay community. : Madam, the changes to the veto and entrenchment framework will further strengthen the governance of the country, providing clarity on the process for Parliamentary override to avoid Government gridlocks and not to create an alternative power centre.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: These changes ensure a safeguard for Singaporeans to be assured that an irresponsible or profligate government does not raid our Reserves.

sections.label: Elected Presidency safeguards against gridlocks
sections.summary: The Elected Presidency framework is being evolved with enhanced safeguards to prevent gridlocks, and the Elected President cannot block the Government from functioning.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The Elected Presidency framework is being evolved with enhanced safeguards to prevent gridlocks and, certainly, the Elected President does not have the powers to block the Government from functioning.

sections.label: Elected Senate versus CPA
sections.summary: The Prime Minister said the CPA has constraints, so electing a CPA is no different from electing an eight-man Senate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: On the elected Senate, how different is it from the CPA, apart from the election?

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The Prime Minister has mentioned earlier in his speech that the CPA has certain constraints.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Therefore, if you want to elect a CPA, it is no different from electing your eight-man Senate.

sections.label: Elected President's moral authority
sections.summary: Trust in the Elected President's judgement lies in his moral authority, which can only be earned by being elected, not appointed, as Head of State.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: And this is why our trust and faith in the Elected President's judgement lies in his moral authority.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: This moral authority, as the Prime Minister has mentioned earlier, can only be earned by being elected by the people, and not appointed, as the Head of State.

sections.label: Elected President settled 25 years ago
sections.summary: The issue of having an Elected President was settled 25 years ago through two White Papers in 1988 and 1991 and the 1988 general elections.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Third, in any case, the issue of whether or not we should have an Elected President was in fact settled 25 years ago.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
