sentences.text: It was settled 25 years ago when two White Papers were put to this House in 1988 and again in 1991 and, eventually, passed in this House.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: And it was one of the platforms on which the 1988 GEs were run and Singaporeans voted on it.

sections.label: Process timing and submissions
sections.summary: It has been close to 10 to 11 months since the Prime Minister raised the question, and 107 submissions were invited and received, including from the WP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Ms Sylvia Lim has also suggested that this has been rushed through, the process has been taken very quickly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: It has been close to 10 to 11 months since the Prime Minister first raised this question in this House at the start of Parliament in January.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: A hundred and seven submissions were invited and received, including from the WP.

sections.label: Elected President's CPA nominees
sections.summary: The Elected President has three nominees onto the CPA and can nominate the Chairman, who has a casting vote.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: The Elected President has three nominees onto the CPA, plus the ability to nominate the Chairman who has a casting vote.

sections.label: Commission casting vote supermajority
sections.summary: The Commission considered that if the Chairman used a casting vote, the Parliamentary override should be a three-quarters supermajority, which was not accepted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In fact, the Commission specifically considered this point and took the position that, in fact, if that happens, if the Chairman had to use his casting vote, then the Parliamentary override should be a higher supermajority of three-quarters, and that was not accepted.

sections.label: Updating CEO qualifying criterion
sections.summary: A criterion requiring 25 years as CEO of a company with $100 million paid-up capital needs updating, as the smallest top 0.2% now has about $431 million.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In that context, having a qualifying criterion that is at least 25 years old based on being a CEO of a company that has a paid-up capital of at least $100 million, that criterion really needs to be updated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Page: 53 If we look at the numbers proffered by the Commission, in 1993, only 0.2% of Singapore incorporated companies met the $100 million paid-up capital requirement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Today, however, the smallest of the top 0.2%, the same percentage of Singapore incorporated companies, we have a paid-up capital of approximately $431 million or more than four times what the threshold was.

sections.label: REACH survey reserved election support
sections.summary: In a REACH survey on reserved elections for minority candidates, 28% of Chinese respondents and at least 40% of Malay and Indian respondents supported it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: And one other number jumped out at me which I would like to share with this House.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: There was the feedback unt Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH) survey and it raised this question: whether there should be a reserved election for minority candidates if a minority member had not been elected President for five terms and so on.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Amongst the Chinese respondents, 28% said they would support such a move.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: But amongst the Malay and Indian respondents, at least 40% said they would support the move.

sections.label: Hiatus-triggered mechanism indigenous creation
sections.summary: The Bill proposes a unique hiatus-triggered mechanism fitting Singapore's historical, social and racial context, which would recede if minority candidates are regularly elected.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Rather, it is an entirely indigenous creation, designed to address the particular imperatives and vulnerabilities in our system of governance against the backdrop of our own historical context." Consistent with our own unique history and that of the Elected President, the Bill now proposes a unique hiatus-triggered mechanism, which I think, after much consideration, does fit into our own historical, social and racial context.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: I would also add that the beauty of this mechanism is that it would entirely recede into insignificance and into the background if candidates from the minority groups are regularly elected Page: 55 into office.

sections.label: Constitutional Commission dual roles tension
sections.summary: More than 20 years after 1998, the Constitutional Commission noted tension in the office's dual roles and a possible need to look at it in future.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: He mentioned earlier that the issue of whether to have an Elected President or not had been settled in the 1998 GEs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: But does he not agree that more than 20 years have passed since then and, importantly, the Constitutional Commission had actually gone out of its way to note that having seen the office in operation, there now seem to be a tension in these dual roles, and that there may be a need to look at it in the future.

sections.label: Enhancements not referendum today
sections.summary: The issue is whether to implement enhancements to powers, revised criteria and the hiatus-triggered mechanism, not whether to hold a referendum today on the Elected President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The point I am making, simply, is that: in this debate, in this Bill, the question of whether the Elected President should or should not be there is not the issue.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The issue today is whether or not the enhancements to the powers, the revision to the criteria, as well as the hiatus-triggered mechanism should be implemented and put into the Constitution.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: To that extent, that is why I said that it is not on the table as to whether or not you should now, today, have a referendum to decide on whether or not to continue with the office of the Elected President through your referendum.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I am not ruling it out, but that is not for today.

sections.label: WP calls for referendum
sections.summary: The WP has called for a referendum on the change from Parliamentary democracy to the Elected President, the second such call.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In fact, on the issue of the change of the political model from a purely Parliamentary democracy Page: 57 inherited from the UK to the one that we have now, the Elected President, the issue has been set out by the WP at the very beginning when the Elected President's idea was mooted and debated publicly in the 1980s.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This is the second time the WP has called for a referendum on the change of political model.

sections.label: Referendum on entrenched provisions
sections.summary: Because changing entrenched Elected Presidency provisions requires a two-third majority in a referendum, a referendum should be held now.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Moreover, as what Ms Sylvia Lim has said, when certain provisions in the Elected Presidency are entrenched, if you want to change it, it will require a two-third majority in a referendum.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: So, I think it is logical that since you want to have a change in the Constitution that requires, if there is a further amendment to that provision, a two-third majority in the referendum, we should have a referendum to make sure that Singaporeans agree today.

sections.label: Stringent candidate conditions
sections.summary: The stringent conditions for candidates ensure the elected President will be a pro-PAP person.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Very obviously, the stringent conditions required of the candidates are to ensure that whoever eventually is elected to be the President will be a pro-PAP person.

sections.label: President won by 1%
sections.summary: The candidate eventually elected President won by a majority of not more than 1% of the votes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Furthermore, the candidate who was eventually elected to be the President, won by a majority of not more than 1% of the votes.

sections.label: Amendment raises qualifying criteria
sections.summary: The amendment Bill raises the qualifying criteria of Presidential Election candidates, reducing the number of eligible candidates.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: First, the amendment Bill raises the qualifying criteria of the Presidential Election candidates, thereby reducing the number of eligible candidates.

sections.label: Ong Pang Boon on Elected Presidency
sections.summary: Ong Pang Boon said the White Paper aimed to ensure a PAP candidate would be elected, and the Bill enhanced the CPA's power.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Former Minister Ong Pang Boon said during a Parliamentary debate on 12 August 1988, "No matter how you look it, the recommendation in the White Paper on Elected Presidency, is aimed at making sure a PAP candidate would be elected, so that in the event another party wins the next GE, he could unseat the new Prime Minister and his government, even when the new government is a responsible government." Furthermore, for fear that the Elected President would not follow its instructions after being elected, the PAP has also enhanced the power of the CPA through this amendment Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Should the President and the majority of Presidential advisors hold the same views, Parliament will have no right to overthrow the joint decision of the President and the CPA.

sections.label: WP proposes Senate replacing Elected Presidency
sections.summary: The WP suggests a Senate replace the Elected Presidency and exercise the President's and CPA's powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: As such, the WP suggests setting up a Senate to replace the Elected Presidency, to exercise the powers of the President and the CPA.

sections.label: Senate veto overruled by government
sections.summary: The Senate's veto can only be overruled by the government with a three-quarter majority in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Under such circumstances, the veto by the Senate can only be overruled by the government with a three-quarter majority in Parliament.

sections.label: WP proposes referendum on two proposals
sections.summary: The WP says a public referendum should decide between the PAP White Paper solution and the WP solution.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The WP holds the view that in dealing with such a major reform to our political system and the separation of powers of the various government institutions, it should be decided by a public referendum of the people.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The referendum shall vote on two proposals: one, the solution as tabled by the PAP in the White Paper, and two, the solution by the WP which specifically includes the following points.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: One, the President is the Head of State, to be appointed by Parliament on a majority vote, to represent Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Three, set up a Senate to replace the Elected Presidency and to exercise the veto power of the President and the CPA, including protecting the Reserves and upholding the integrity of the civil servants to be appointed by the government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Four, Parliament can override the veto by the Senate, by way of a three-quarter majority of the total number of Members voting in favour thereof.

sections.label: No Malay President for 50 years
sections.summary: The passage notes there has been no Malay President for close to 50 years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: For a country whose anthem is in our national language, it cannot escape notice that there has been no Malay President for close to 50 years.

sections.label: Reserved election compromises meritocracy
sections.summary: The proposed changes to reserve an election for a minority group come across as compromising on meritocracy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In general, I know that Singaporeans will support a President from any race, but the proposed changes to the Elected Presidency scheme to reserve an election for a minority group comes across as compromising on meritocracy.

sections.label: President safeguards Reserves from populist government
sections.summary: The purpose of electing a president is to make sure someone safeguards the Reserves from a populist government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: The purpose of electing a president in Singapore is to make sure that someone safeguards our Reserves from a populist government.

sections.label: Race equality and presidential amendments
sections.summary: The speaker supports the amendments and the hiatus-triggered principle, and asks that the changes take effect in phases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: It would be naive to think that after just 50 years of nationhood, we are race-blind when it comes to politics.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: It is thus that I support these amendments and, in particular, the hiatus-triggered principle because equality of races is not a given.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: It is because we hold true to that ideal that we must make rules, knowing that we are not playing at some Platonic form of a game, but in the very real world.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: This hiatus-triggered principle is an example of Singapore's semangat yang baru, a legislative innovation that shows how seriously Singapore takes equality among races.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Today, this need to ensure that all races have a part in national life has been corrupted by accusations that the revisions in the law are part of a political chess game.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: So, to gainsay these critics, I ask that the changes come into effect in phases: perhaps, the revised eligibility criteria before the next Presidential Election and the reserved election provision to be only after the next Presidential Election.

sections.label: Presidential candidate eligibility criteria
sections.summary: The speaker suggests considering only Singapore-born candidates, raising the minimum age to 50, and notes about 700 companies remain eligible.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Using the $500 million benchmark, I believe about 700 companies are still eligible to nominate their most senior executives to be the country's next Elected President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Second, I feel that Singapore has now come of age, with a large pool of Singaporeans with deep links and affinity to this country.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Hence, I believe that we should consider only Presidential candidates who are born in Singapore, in contrast to those who have taken up citizenship along the way.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Currently, the required qualifications as stated in our Constitution are: being a citizen of Singapore, and not below the age of 45.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: I feel the candidate's age can be set higher, at not below the age of 50.

sections.label: NCMPs voting rights
sections.summary: The speaker says NCMPs lack the people's mandate, so there is no basis to grant them full voting rights as elected MPs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Given their nominated status, I feel that NCMPs do not have the mandate of the people.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Hence, I am of the view that there is no basis to grant them full voting rights as elected MPs.

sections.label: Racial harmony and Elected President debate
sections.summary: The speaker says deliberate interventions and policies are needed for racial harmony, and addresses confusion between NMPs and NCMPs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: We believe that it takes careful, deliberate and calibrated interventions plus policies on our part to make racial harmony a reality in Singapore and leaving nothing to chance or fate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: I have spoken about the legislative innovations in GEs to keep faith with both the legitimacy that derives from a popular process, while ensuring fairness in this process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In the same way, I consider today's debate on the Elected President as part of our singular and Singaporean way of dealing with race relations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In this and in so much more, we are guided by the phrase which our children pledge themselves to every school day – may our hopes and dreams bring Singapore every success. "Cita-cita kita yang mulia;berjaya Singapura!"

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: I think the Member has confused the Nominated Member (NMP) with the NCMP.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: We are not nominated and we do not represent special interest.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: So, may I know which special interest we could possibly represent?

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Perhaps Mr Seah could give an example, just so we can understand what the concerns he has.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
sentences.text: I do not have any particular issue but I am just stating that there could be different interest groups that may make their cases known to a particular NCMP for them to take up his case.

sections.label: Representing the majority
sections.summary: The speaker states that they represent the majority.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
sentences.text: Well, first of all, we represent the majority.

sections.label: Deliberative track for past presidents
sections.summary: The speaker asks how clause 7(b)'s deliberative track can include past presidents, citing the Distinguished Service Order and the Commission's view.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: They neither ran $500 Page: 66 million companies or equivalents then, nor did they occupy an office that would immediately qualify them even to stand for elections.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: So, I request the Government to explain how the deliberative tracks under clause 7(b) of the Bill will be flexible enough to include men like Mr Wee Kim Wee, Mr Devan Nair, Dr Benjamin Sheares and Encik Yusof Ishak.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: As one example, and just as one example, the description of the Distinguished Service Order, the Darjah Utama Bakti Cemerlang, states, "The Order may be awarded to any person who has performed within Singapore any act or series of acts constituting distinguished conduct." What I am asking for is that the deliberative track through clause 7(b) recognises distinguished conduct for and on behalf of the state.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: This reasoning finds support in the deliberations of the Commission itself, who formed the view that it was not prudent to fetter the PEC's discretion by setting out an exhaustive list of factors that the PEC should consider, save one pertaining to performance, but that the PEC should take a holistic view of the applicant's experience and expertise, and assess whether he is likely to be qualified to hold the office of President.

sections.label: Elected Presidency qualifying criteria flexibility
sections.summary: The speaker asks for flexibility in the deliberative track and cites economic justifications for changing the qualifying criterion to $500 million shareholders' equity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Today, let us not overly restrain ourselves to a qualification criterion that is not wide enough to draw a man or woman whom the body of Singaporeans or the Government believes is needed in years to come.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: It is for this reason that I ask for flexibility in the deliberative track.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Clause 7(b) of the Bill amends Article 19 such that the candidate has to be the most senior executive of a company with $500 million shareholders' equity and who is principally responsible for the running of the company.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: We have heard the economic justifications for the change from $100 million paid-up capital to $500 million shareholders' equity in the form of several arguments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: One, how the number of companies with $100 million paid-up capital has increased between then and now.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Two, how shareholders' equity shows whether a company is a going concern rather than a historic figure which may be all lost.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: And three, how the candidate has to be hands-on, actually involved in the running of the company, rather than just the big picture.

sections.label: Public service record requirement
sections.summary: A qualifying candidate should have a record of public service in addition to running a $500 million company.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Essentially, in addition to running a $500 million company, a qualifying candidate should also have a record of public service.

sections.label: Menon Commission on elected Presidency
sections.summary: After 107 written submissions and oral representations, the Menon Constitutional Commission asked whether the Presidency should remain an elected office.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: After reading 107 written submissions and receiving oral representations from selected contributors, the Menon Constitutional Commission was compelled to ask a critical question, which, in the opinion of the WP, all Singaporeans ought to ponder over seriously, and that is, should the Presidency remain an elected office?

sections.label: President power and mandate statements
sections.summary: Prime Minister Lee said the President cannot be an alternative centre of power, and the Law Minister said the President must be elected to have the popular mandate to veto.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Page: 68 In January this year, when the Prime Minister announced the setting up of a Constitutional Commission to study changes to the Elected Presidency, Prime Minister Lee said that the President cannot be an alternative centre of power.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In September, when the Law Minister rebutted the Constitutional Commission's alternative proposal to replace the Elected Presidency with an appointed Council of Experts, he said that the President himself must be elected to have the popular mandate to veto an elected Government.

sections.label: Disagreement on tightening qualifying criteria
sections.summary: The speaker disagrees with the Government that tightening the Elected Presidency qualifying criteria and strengthening the CPA is the solution.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: To this end, we disagree with the Government that the solution to the current problem is to tighten the qualifying criteria of the Elected Presidency and to strengthen the CPA).

sections.label: Expanding CPA beyond advisory function
sections.summary: Expanding the CPA to eight members and obliging consultation on reserves and key appointments changes the CPA beyond its advisory function.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: By expanding the CPA from six to eight members and obliging the President to consult the Council on all monetary matters related to the reserves and all key Public Service appointments, the Government is not Page: 69 merely strengthening the CPA's advisory capacity, but is changing the very nature of the CPA beyond its advisory function.

sections.label: Reserved election and Senate proposal
sections.summary: The Government's reserved election proposal does not solve the problem, and the WP proposes a ceremonial Presidency with an Elected Senate, while the Commission's alternative is an appointed Presidency with experts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Government's proposal to reserve an election for an ethnic community, if the past five Elected Presidents did not come from that ethnic community, does not solve the problem.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Over a long period, our Presidents should come from the main ethnic communities to symbolise and express the multiracial fabric of our nation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: As the ethnicity of the candidates will be pushed into the glare of competitive elections in the case of reserved elections, this will inadvertently lead to the politicisation of multiracialism and may even introduce communal interests into the contest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Thirdly, the WP proposes to revert to the ceremonial Presidency and to establish an Elected Senate to fulfil the custodial role as the solution.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: We studied and deliberated the Constitutional Commission's report and agreed that the most elegant solution to the problem is the Commission's alternative proposal to revert to an appointed ceremonial Presidency and to set up a group of experts to exercise the Elected President's custodial role.

sections.label: Elected Senate under Option B
sections.summary: The WP proposes an elected Senate as an Upper House with eight Senators elected from a list, exercising the Elected President's custodial functions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The second, titled Checks and Balances under Option B, presents a streamlined system of checks and balances with an elected Senate, as put forth by the WP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: We propose that a Senate be established within our Legislature as an Upper House to exercise the custodial functions that are now exercised by the Elected President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: Eight Senators shall be elected from a list in periodic elections where non-partisan candidates will have to fit the qualifying criteria.

sections.label: Senate veto and Parliament override
sections.summary: A Senate veto returns relevant Bills to Parliament, which can override it with a 75% or three-quarters majority.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: A Senate veto will return relevant Bills to Parliament for debate, which Parliament can veto with a 75% or three-quarters majority.

sections.label: Referendum on constitutional amendments
sections.summary: The WP views the proposed constitutional amendments as major changes that should not be made hastily and should be put to a referendum.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: Fourthly, the WP is of the view that the proposed constitutional amendments are major changes that should not be made with indecent haste and should be put to a referendum.

sections.label: Frequency of Senate elections
sections.summary: Senate elections are seen every six years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: In the first case, as to how often we see Senate elections, we see them every six years.

sections.label: Senate election nomination criteria
sections.summary: The Senate Elections Committee would take the form and substance of the current PEC, with the same six individuals assessing who qualifies to be on the Senate.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
sentences.text: What would be the criteria to be nominated for election?

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: We see the Senate Elections Committee really taking on the form and substance of the current PEC So, the same individuals will determine which individuals can stand for Senate elections and, for the same reason, those six individuals, we believe, would be able to put their minds to assessing who ought to qualify to be on the Senate.

sections.label: PEC narrowing applicants to 16
sections.summary: The PEC follows its mandate and must narrow the slate of applicants down to 16.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: Like I mentioned, it really follows the mandate that is given to the PEC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: But the main point is that they will have to narrow down the slate of applicants to the number 16.

sections.label: Senate Committee selecting 16 candidates
sections.summary: The Senate Elections Committee must draw a line, pick 16 best qualified individuals, and citizens then whittle the list to eight.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: The issue is, at the point, before the process becomes unwieldy, the Senate Elections Committee has to draw a line.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: And it will have to determine for the 16 individuals that it has decided upon who are the best qualified for that job and, after that, when it goes to the polls, the citizens of Singapore will whittle that list further down to eight, basically.

sections.label: Preserving President's symbolic unifying role
sections.summary: The question is whether to preserve the President's symbolic and unifying role and have an elected Senate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: The question is, do we want to preserve the symbolic and unifying role of the President, and by doing that have an elected Senate which we will, of course, have to persuade the public, "Look, these are my credentials, I am a Singaporean and I seek to play my role as part of a legislative member".

sections.label: Diversity under WP's elected proposal
sections.summary: The WP proposal raises how diversity from business experience, civil servants and judges would be obtained in a purely elected system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: In the WP's proposal, when it is just an election, how then do you get the kind of diversity, such as you have the people with business experience or civil servants who know how the Government runs, judges who know how to interpret the law?

sentences.speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
sentences.text: Yes, they can stand, but how it works is that, currently, because they are appointed, the diversity helps in giving a different perspective and a more rounded decision-making.

sections.label: Senate identifying suitable individuals
sections.summary: The Senate must identify individuals able to perform the role expected of Senators, and Reserve drawdowns would go to the Senate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: It will have to put its mind to identifying individuals who it believes would be able to perform the role expected of Senators.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
sentences.text: I believe the Member said just now that if there is a gridlock in the Senate, the decision will be passed back down to Parliament.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
sentences.text: In that case, why would Parliament float the matter up to the Senate in the first place?

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: Well, it would have to go to the Senate by virtue of the fact that that would be the process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: So, if the government of the day wants to draw down on the Reserves, then, by its very nature, it would go to the Senate.

sections.label: Elected President's 1991 constitutional powers
sections.summary: Constitutional amendments in 1991 created the Elected President as chief public representative and non-partisan custodian with fiscal discretionary powers and veto over key appointments.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Constitutional amendments were made through an amendment in 1991, as we know, based on two White Papers, one Select Committee Report and extensive Parliamentary debates.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Not only is the Elected President real to the people now as Singapore's chief public representative, as someone that they can cast their vote at the ballot box for, but he can also become our non-partisan custodian, as he is.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: He is endowed with discretionary powers over a range of fiscal matters and has the power to veto any proposed appointment or removal of key office holders in the Public Service.

sections.label: White Paper on Elected President
sections.summary: The speaker notes the latest White Paper responds to the report and forms the basis of the amendment Bill, and says the President should remain elected with an appointed CPA.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I have also seen the latest White Paper in this regard which responds to the report and forms the basis of this amendment Page: 76 Bill.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is clear to me, Madam, that the President should remain an elected office and his CPA should be appointed.

sections.label: Teo and Tony Tan speeches
sections.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Teo said the amendments would help avoid gridlock when the President and Government disagree, and President Tony Tan said the Elected President cannot be hamstrung.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo said yesterday in the Second Reading speech that the amendments would, among other things, "help to avoid gridlock in situations where the President and the Government do not agree".

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: President Tony Tan's message to this House before that Second Reading speech was powerful, Madam.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: He said, among other things, "We cannot hamstring the Elected President.

sections.label: Constitutional Commission Report findings
sections.summary: Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon's Constitutional Commission Report noted about one third of constitutional amendment Acts from 1991 to 2007 concerned the Elected Presidency, half on fiscal powers.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon's Constitutional Commission Report noted that approximately one third of all the constitutional amendment Acts passed between 1991 and 2007 concerned the Elected Presidency, and that half of those amendments were directed at the President's fiscal powers.

sections.label: Nathan's 2008 deposit guarantee
sections.summary: In October 2008, the month this House last spoke about entrenching the President's powers, President Nathan willingly exercised his discretion and approved a $150 billion guarantee on bank deposits backed by Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Indeed, it is only now that we know that in the very month that this House last spoke about entrenchment of the President's powers in 2008, President Nathan had in that same month, October 2008, willingly exercised his discretion.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: He had approved a $150 billion guarantee on all bank deposits to be backed by our Reserves.

sections.label: President's moral authority and CPA
sections.summary: The speaker agrees an electoral mandate gives the President moral authority as a second key with the Prime Minister and Cabinet as the first, and asks whether the President must be their professional equal to deal with the CPA.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Although I agree with the Government that an electoral mandate gives the President the moral authority to act as a second key, with the Prime Minister and the Cabinet as the first, I ask this: is it the Government's position that to deal with the CPA, the President, too, must be their professional equal?

sections.label: PEC reasons under Article 19
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether under the new Article 19 the PEC will be required or encouraged to give reasons on whether a person has the experience and ability to carry out the Office's functions.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Under the new Article 19, will the PEC be required or encouraged to provide reasons for its decisions on whether the discretionary limb, that is, "whether a person has the experience and ability to effectively carry out the functions and duties of the Office"?

sections.label: Council of Experts second Chamber
sections.summary: A Council of Experts as a second Chamber of Parliament could delay measures, force debates and require a supermajority to override objections.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: A Council of Experts as a second Chamber of Parliament with the ability to delay measures, force a debate upon them and require the Government to override any objections only with a supermajority, was what they said.

sections.label: Ombudsman proposal deferred 1966
sections.summary: In 1966 the Law Minister EW Barker said creating an Ombudsman should be deferred until results of experiments in New Zealand and elsewhere.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: When it was raised in 1966 to the Wee Chong Jin Commission, the response by the Law Minister at that time Mr EW Barker was this.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: He said, "The creation of the Ombudsman or the Parliamentary Commissioner on the lines of the recommendations of this Commission should be deferred until the results of the experiment in New Zealand and elsewhere." The reason for this was, at that time, it was only in the UK that had preferred to have a Parliamentary Commissioner.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Fifty years later, the Parliamentary Commissioner in New Zealand has been hailed a success, Madam.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I would argue that we should, if nothing else, study the feasibility of including this within our system in due course.

sections.label: Upper House question 1999
sections.summary: In 1999 Minister Wong Kan Seng said Singapore's unicameral Parliament has worked well and already has nine nominated non-elected Members.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In 1999, in reply to Mr Srinivas Rai's question on whether the Government will consider setting up an Upper House, Mr Wong Kan Seng, who was Minister for Home Affairs at that time, said, "In our unicameral Parliament, which has worked well, there are already nine nominated non-elected Members in this House.

sections.label: Support for minority representation
sections.summary: A speaker from another minority group fully supports it, saying minorities must be ensured a representative in the highest office.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As a person from another minority group, I would like to now say that I fully support it.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is important for minorities to be ensured of a representative in the highest office of the country.

sections.label: Elected President qualifying criteria
sections.summary: New qualifying criteria do not require wealth but a capable, responsible steward, with the Elected Presidency institutionalising self-discipline.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Even though the "steward" of a company is not managing his own money, he is still committed to his responsibilities.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Therefore, the new qualifying criteria for the Elected President does not mean that he has to be wealthy.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: The new criteria mean that the Elected President must be a good "steward" who is capable and responsible.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: However, we cannot rely solely on an individual's sense of responsibility.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: That is why we have the Elected Presidency, and we have institutionalised this spirit of self-discipline to ensure that our Page: 82 wealth can last beyond three generations.

sections.label: Numbers meeting new criteria
sections.summary: Figures show more people meet the new criteria to run for President than in the 1990s, and future candidates may differ from the ruling party.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: In fact, figures show that the number of people who meet the new criteria to run for President now is even more than that in the 1990s.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: In future, there will definitely be presidential candidates who meet the new criteria, but with views different from that of the ruling party.

sections.label: Elected President and CPA
sections.summary: The passage states concern that an elected government may misuse the Reserves or appoint aides or friends to key positions, and that an Elected President assisted by a CPA, not a cumbersome senate, is needed to prevent this.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Our concern is that Page: 83 an elected government may misuse the Reserves, or appoint aides or friends to key positions in the government.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: To prevent such a situation, we need an Elected President who is assisted by a CPA, not a cumbersome senate.

sections.label: Minority candidate capability concern
sections.summary: The passage states concern that if a minority candidate wins a term reserved for minorities, people may focus only on minority status and overlook that the person is capable.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Instead, they are concerned that if a minority candidate wins a particular term of the Elected Presidency that is reserved for minorities, will people focus only on the fact that he or she is from the minority and overlook the fact that he or she is, indeed, a capable individual?

sections.label: Elected President reserves experience
sections.summary: The passage states that if the Reserves are to be well-protected, the Elected President needs relevant experience in managing a large organisation.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: By the same logic, if we want our Reserves to be well-protected, the Elected President will need to have relevant experience in managing a large organisation.

sections.label: Checks from enhanced Parliament
sections.summary: The passage states that checks were accepted, but checks from a Parliament having an enhanced majority.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: You accepted that there should be checks, but checks from a Parliament having an enhanced majority.

sections.label: Eligibility criteria and minority mechanism
sections.summary: The passage states that the eligibility criteria for the Elected Presidency should be raised with time and economic growth, and a mechanism should ensure minorities can be President, in line with multiracial Singapore principles.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: The eligibility criteria for the Elected Presidency should be raised, together with time and economic growth.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Second, let us put in place a mechanism to ensure that minorities can be President, in line with our principles of a multiracial Singapore.

sections.label: Positions on Elected Presidency safeguards
sections.summary: The passage states that from the 1980s to date the fundamentals are the same: disagreement with the Elected Presidency and belief it should be abolished, and agreement that additional safeguards on past Reserves should vest in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: Actually, if we look at our positions from the 1980s to date, the fundamentals are still the same, as in: one, we do not agree with the Elected Presidency and we believe that it should be abolished – that position has not changed; and two, we have always agreed that there should be additional safeguards on our past Reserves, and that safeguard should vest in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: So, in that regard, the proposal that we have today about having an elected Senate, Members will recall that we said that there should be a second chamber in the legislature.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: And in any case, if the matter is not agreed to by the Senate, it will come back to Parliament to be passed by a supermajority.

sections.label: WP manifesto on Parliament power
sections.summary: A speaker seeks clarification on Ms Sylvia Lim's statement that the WP manifesto said Parliament's power should be unfettered.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: I seek a clarification on what Ms Sylvia Lim said.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: I think in the manifesto last year, the WP said, "Power of Parliament, as the people's representative, should be unfettered".

sections.label: WP submission on Elected President
sections.summary: The passage reads the WP's submission, which agrees large Reserves should be safeguarded but says the Elected President is not the right mechanism.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: And since the Minister quoted from our submission to the Commission, I can read to Members what we said.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: We said that, "We agree that large Reserves built up in the past should be safeguarded, but we believe the Elected President is not the right mechanism for this.

sections.label: Supermajority versus elected Senate
sections.summary: The passage contrasts a parliamentary supermajority to use Reserves with an elected Senate of 16 contesting and eight elected.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Supermajority in Parliament to use Reserves, as opposed to having an elected Senate with 16 people contesting and eight people being elected.

sections.label: Sixteen candidates and Senate committee
sections.summary: The passage states that, as understood from Mr Pritam Singh, there will be 16 candidates and a committee acting like the PEC.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: As I understood earlier from Mr Pritam Singh, there will be 16 candidates − the criteria would be like, I suppose, a Senate election committee which will act like the PEC and operate like the PEC.

sections.label: Senate Elections Committee shortlists candidates
sections.summary: The passage states that the SEC, the Senate Elections Committee, has to shortlist 16 candidates.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The SEC − let us call it the Senate Elections Committee, the SEC – has got to shortlist 16 candidates.

sections.label: Senate selection and election process
sections.summary: The passage describes the SEC reviewing applicants on eligibility criteria, ranking 16 candidates, and a senatorial election electing eight from that ballot.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: It would consider applicants who would like to run for the office of Senator.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: It would review those applications with those eligibility criteria in mind, that is, financial management capability, human resources and so on, criteria that one needs to play a custodial role and it would rank the 16 most suitable and most eligible candidates to go on to the ballot and, from that, the senatorial election would then elect eight candidates from a ballot of 16.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Will they, the candidates, need to, for example, have run companies of the size as set out currently in the requirements?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: It would be part of the criteria to be considered, and that would be an advantage in the selection process.

sections.label: Similar criteria comparison
sections.summary: The criteria would be similar, but something would not be similar.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: The criteria would be similar but what would not be similar ─

sections.label: Custodial role to Senate
sections.summary: The custodial role is transferred from an Elected President to a Senate, with 16 qualified people contesting.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: So, it is transferring the custodial role from an Elected President to a Senate.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, we will have 16 people who are qualified to be Elected Presidents, who will have to contest.

sections.label: SEC choosing top 16
sections.summary: Under the proposal, the SEC chooses the top 16, which is not justiciable and entirely within their discretion.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Under your proposal, the SEC will choose the top 16, and this is not justiciable, Mr Singh told us.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, it is entirely in their discretion to choose 16 people who will submit their names.

sections.label: Sixteen-person limit and shortfall
sections.summary: The SEC limits selection to 16 people, while the Government's proposal could allow more, and it asks what happens if fewer than eight qualify or stand.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: In respect of that, they choose 16 people and they limit it to 16 people, whereas the proposal of the Government could, in theory, as the Minister rightly pointed out, be far more than 16, it could be 100 if 100 people meet those criteria, yes, that is correct.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And what happens if less than eight people qualify or stand?

sections.label: Global political disunity and far-right
sections.summary: The US and UK show public disunity, while far-right parties gain traction in Finland, Sweden, Austria, Germany and France.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Both the US and the UK are going through an unprecedented public display of disunity at the government as well as the ground level.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In Finland, Sweden, Austria, Germany and France, far-right parties are gaining in political traction with the electorate with uncomfortable ease, and racist and xenophobic political agendas have become normalised.

sections.label: Politicians meeting across partisan divides
sections.summary: Given global events, politicians should meet across partisan divides to examine the union and build checks and balances.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Given the backdrop of current global events, I am reminded that there is no better time than now for our own politicians to meet across partisan divides to look – to really look – at the state of our own union, to build our own system's circuit breakers, to fight for the checks and balances we most believe in.

sections.label: President's unifying multiracial role
sections.summary: The speaker accepts the Government's reserved election option to keep the Presidency accessible to all major races.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Presently, the discussion of this particular unifying role of the President is centred purely on multiracial representation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: And I have no quarrel with the Government's decision to go for a reserved election option to ensure that the Presidency is accessible to all the major races in Singapore.

sections.label: US racism as systemic problem
sections.summary: The speaker says racism is systemic and cannot be fixed by minority representation in the highest office.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Page: 97 Some political scientists have argued that the political dysfunctions we are witnessing right now in America have less to do with race and more to do with class divides, partisan politics and a divisive electoral process.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: And the reminder I will take from the US presidential election is that racism is a systemic problem that cannot be fixed simply by minority representation in the highest office of the land.

sections.label: US income inequality figures
sections.summary: The top 1% in the US earned 9% of income in 1979 and almost 25% today, with over 90% of 2010 income gains going to them.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In 1979, the top 1% in the US earned 9% of its income; today they earn almost 25%.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In 2010, more than 90% of the country's income gains went to the top 1%.

sections.label: Hesitation over eligibility criteria
sections.summary: The speaker brings three requests and remains hesitant to support stricter eligibility criteria for the Elected Presidency.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But I will still bring three requests today to the table.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I am still hesitant to support the new stricter set of eligibility criteria for the Elected Presidency.

sections.label: Doubts on stricter criteria
sections.summary: The speaker is unsure whether stricter criteria sieve in good candidates or slant the Presidency towards public sector and minority candidates.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is just that I am unsure whether having such criteria now will help us sieve in more good candidates or sieve out more promising ones.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I am unsure whether stricter private sector criteria will end up slanting our Presidency towards more public sector candidates, especially in the case of minority candidates.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: How drastic is the difference between CEOs who lead $500 million organisations and CEOs who lead $100 million or $300 million organisations in terms of their intellectual competency, financial proficiency, moral courage and diplomatic sensitivity?

sections.label: Reviewing criteria strictness
sections.summary: The speaker requests relooking the strictness of criteria, warning that uncontested or homogeneous elections harm democracy.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The latter duty demands no less rigour than the former.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I request that we consider relooking the strictness of criteria, especially if we start to see either a recurring pattern of uncontested elections due to lack of eligible private sector candidates or a recurring pattern of elections dominated only by public sector candidates.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: A string of uncontested elections or even elections with homogeneous establishment candidates harms our democracy as it only feeds into a dangerous narrative of a "rigged system" that entrenches either cynicism or apathy among the electorate.

sections.label: Reconsidering an electoral college
sections.summary: The speaker believes it is worth reconsidering, further down the road, the 2011 suggestion by Mr Janadas Devan and Mr Ho Kwon Ping to establish an electoral college.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Personally, I believe further down the road, it is worth reconsidering what Mr Janadas Devan and Mr Ho Kwon Ping suggested in 2011 about establishing an electoral college instead.

sections.label: Clearer rules for 2017 elections
sections.summary: The speaker says taking that right away now would not go down well and thinks the next best thing for now is clearer rules of engagement for the 2017 Presidential Elections.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, to take that right away now would not go down well either.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I do think the next best thing to do, for now, would be to establish clearer rules of engagement for the upcoming 2017 Presidential Elections.

sections.label: Ombudsman to depoliticise Presidency
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the Government can consider setting up an ombudsman to take on the interventionist role some voters want in the President's role.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Another way to depoliticise the Presidency is to provide other democratic institutions that can take on the more interventionist role that some voters want to shoe-horn into the President's role even though it conflicts with his need to symbolise national unity.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, can the Government consider setting up the institution of an ombudsman to take that up?

sections.label: Eligibility criteria and people-sector leaders
sections.summary: The speaker says the eligibility criteria mean only public or private sector experience prepares a President, and people-sector leaders would find the deliberative track almost impossible.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Going by the eligibility criteria, only experience and expertise in the public or private sector prepare an individual to be a President of Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Even though there is a deliberative track, it Page: 100 would be really difficult and almost impossible to find a leader from our local landscape of voluntary welfare groups, non-profit charities, philanthropic foundations and carts or cultural groups who can say their organisations are of equivalent size and complexity as a $500 million company or a Government agency.

sections.label: Not asking for easier shot
sections.summary: The speaker says this is not about simplistically asking for people-sector leaders to be given an easier shot at running for the Presidency.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This is not about simplistically asking for people sector leaders to be given an easier shot at running for the Presidency.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I accept that the President's custodial role of safeguarding our national Reserves demands a level of financial sophistication and organisational expertise that is likely to be beyond the scope of most people-sector leaders.

sections.label: People-sector space in PEC and CPA
sections.summary: The speaker requests that space be made somehow for leaders from the people sector in the composition of the PEC and the CPA.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Can I request that in the composition of the PEC as well as the CPA, we make a space somehow for leaders from the people sector?

sections.label: Constitution must stay ever new
sections.summary: A Constitution must be protected for stability yet flexible enough to stay relevant to each new generation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Franklin Roosevelt once said that a Constitution should be revered "not because it is old, but because it is ever new, not in the worship of its past alone but in the faith of the living who keep it young, now and in the years to come." A Constitution must be protected enough to ensure stability from government to government but it must also have enough breathing room to be a living, vital thing, evolving enough such that it remains relevant to the needs of every new generation.

sections.label: Elected Presidency and reserved election
sections.summary: The speaker calls for unity, restates opposition to the Elected Presidency and asks about reserved Presidential Elections for minorities.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Let us please work together to bring down walls, protect the state of our union and find a way for Singapore to be a small but strong and powerful light of unity even in the darkness of a divided world.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: We would like to state that we stand by our original position we had since the office of the Elected Presidency was instituted, that is, we do not agree with the Elected Presidency and call for the Presidency to be returned to its original office, that is, an appointed Presidency.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I would also like to touch on whether it is necessary to have a reserved Presidential Election so that minorities have the chance to become the President.

sections.label: Tension between election and unifying role
sections.summary: The Government accepted tension between the election process and the Elected President's unifying role, and the speaker asks two questions of Deputy Prime Minister Teo.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: First, the Government accepted that there are tensions between the election process and the role of the Elected President as the unifier of the nation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: With regard to this argument, I have two questions for Deputy Prime Minister Teo.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: First, on what basis does the Government believe that this tension can be mitigated and, second, what will the Government do to mitigate this tension?

sections.label: Commission's proposed second chamber
sections.summary: The Commission proposed an appointed body of experts as a second chamber with a process-delaying role, while the Government believes the second key needs an electoral mandate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Commission conceptualised this appointed body as a body of experts that will be the second chamber of Parliament, that is, given a process-delaying role, by forcing something to be debated again and requiring the Government to override any objections only with a supermajority.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: First, the Government believes that the second key must be held by an institution that has obtained the direct mandate from Singaporeans through an election process.

sections.label: Commission view on appointed Presidency
sections.summary: The Constitutional Commission, set up by the Prime Minister and comprising individuals without political interests, views that the Presidency should revert to an appointed office.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Constitutional Commission, that was set up by the Prime Minister himself and comprising individuals who do not have any political interests, is of the view that the Presidency should revert to an appointed office, with the concern that this can avoid something undesirable from happening in the future, that is, society being divided and political conflict occurs between the President and the Government.

sections.label: Elected Senate and reserved Malay election
sections.summary: The speaker suggests a custodial role for an elected eight-person chamber or Senate and asks Deputy Prime Minister Teo about a reserved election only for Malay candidates.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, there is some difference between our proposals and the Commission's proposal about the custodial role.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: We suggest that this role be given to a chamber or Senate comprising eight individuals who are elected via a national election process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Another thing that I would touch on is about the suggestion to have a reserved Presidential Election for minorities so that they have the chance to become President.Sir, I have two questions for Deputy Prime Minister Teo on the Government's plan to have a reserved election only for Malay candidates.

sections.label: Eight elected individuals versus one President
sections.summary: The speaker says they believe eight elected individuals will do a better job than one Elected President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
sentences.text: What I can say is that we believe the basic, the fundamental, is that these eight elected individuals will do a better job than one Elected President.

sections.label: Elected Senators as better option
sections.summary: The speaker says they do not agree totally, but view elected Senators as better than an unelected body for moral authority and people's mandate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
sentences.text: I did not say that we agree with them totally.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
sentences.text: Hence, we have our own views whereby we said that the elected Senators are a better option than a body that is not elected, in order to retain its moral authority and also to receive the mandate from the people.

sections.label: Rotational system for appointed Presidency
sections.summary: The speaker says minority chances of becoming President can be resolved by a rotational system for the appointed Presidency.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
sentences.text: As I stated earlier, we do not discount the importance of taking care of Malay issues or giving the Presidency to the Malays.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
sentences.text: We did say that the issue of minorities not having a chance to Page: 109 become a President can be resolved by having a rotational system for the appointed Presidency.

sections.label: Appointed President scheme and Malay servicemen
sections.summary: The speaker says minority Presidency can be addressed by reverting to appointed President, and notes Malay National Servicemen serve in Navy ships with dietary provisions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
sentences.text: What I mentioned is that instead of allowing the minority to hold the office of Presidency, it can be addressed by reverting to the appointed President scheme.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: He alluded to the halal kitchen, implying that there are no Malay National Servicemen serving in the Navy ships.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: I am just wondering if he is aware that there are actually Malay National Servicemen serving in our Navy ships and provisions are made where possible to provide them with their dietary requirements.

sections.label: Bill on multi-racial Presidency representation
sections.summary: The speaker notes agreement and says the Bill proposes constitutional changes including a mechanism for multi-racial representation for the Elected Presidency.

sentences.speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
sentences.text: Okay, I am glad to see that there is agreement on that point.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
sentences.text: This Bill relates to the proposed changes to our Constitution, which include, amongst other things, having a mechanism to ensure multi-racial representation for the Office of the Elected Presidency.

sections.label: Reserved Presidential Election and five-term gap
sections.summary: The Bill provides a reserved Presidential Election if no community member has held the Office for five terms; the speaker asks if five terms is too long.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
sentences.text: One of the amendments proposed in this Bill is to provide for a Presidential Election to be reserved for a community if no person belonging to that community has held the Office of President for five presidential terms.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
sentences.text: Page: 111 Deputy Speaker, Sir, our President is a symbol of our national identity, representing all Singaporeans, and multiracialism is an important aspect of Singapore's social fabric and remains fundamental to our unity and survival.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
sentences.text: I agree with the introduction of the hiatus-triggered mechanism to ensure minority representation in our highest office.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
sentences.text: However, is a gap of five presidential terms, which is about 30 years, considered too long?

sentences.speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
sentences.text: I hope the Government would monitor public sentiments in this respect and to make the appropriate adjustments in future, if necessary.

sections.label: Reserved Presidential Elections racial lines
sections.summary: Asks whether reserving Presidential Elections to racial groups best helps the Elected President unify Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Does an enforced reservation of Presidential Elections to particular groups of Singaporeans defined along racial lines best help the Elected President play a unifying role?

sections.label: Costs of tightened eligibility criteria
sections.summary: States tightened eligibility criteria reduce the number of possible Presidents when good candidates are hard to find.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But these tightened eligibility criteria have their own costs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
sentences.text: They reduce the number of men and women who could be President at a time when we understand that good men and women for the job are so hard to find.

sections.label: Former Presidents and eligibility criteria
sections.summary: Asks how many former Presidents would be ineligible and whether Elected Presidents behaved untowardly needing corrective action.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
sentences.text: With the proposed tightened eligibility criteria, how many of our former Presidents – Yusof Ishak, Benjamin Sheares, Devan Nair, Wee Kim Wee – would have been found ineligible to serve, even if they were ready and eager to do so, and in the eyes of vast numbers of Singaporeans, be qualified to do so?

sentences.speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Has any of our Elected Presidents – Ong Teng Cheong, SR Nathan and Tony Tan – behaved so untowardly that we feel corrective action is needed to limit the number of eligible candidates from, say, qualifying companies with paid-in capital of at least $100 million, to those with shareholders' equity of at least $500 million?

sections.label: Restricting non-executive chairmen candidates
sections.summary: Asks why custodial functions justify eliminating non-executive chairmen of eligible companies, who qualified under current rules.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Even just looking at the custodial functions of the President, why are we seeking to restrict further the number of men and women who could be President by eliminating the non-executive chairmen of eligible companies from consideration, where both the chairmen and the chief executive officers used to qualify under the current rules?

sections.label: NCMPs serving in Town Councils
sections.summary: States NCMPs can serve in a Town Council but are not required to, unlike elected MPs.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: The NCMP can serve in a Town Council, they are not required to, unlike an elected MP, but all kinds of people can serve in a Town Council and can be appointed by MPs, including NCMPs from the same party.

sections.label: Senate and custodial powers
sections.summary: Says some do not support the Presidency yet devolve the President's custodial powers to eight senators.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Again and again, we hear about the elections for a Senate, the senators.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: They say they do not support the Presidency but yet they are taking the custodial powers of the President and devolving it to eight senators.

sections.label: Collective wisdom and Presidential system overhaul
sections.summary: The only reason given was the wisdom of a crowd, and it is a major overhaul of the Presidential and possibly political system.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: The only reason they had given is this "wisdom of a crowd", I believe it was the phrase that was used, or "the collective wisdom", that somehow, automatically, collective wisdom is better.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: It is a major overhaul of our entire Presidential system and, possibly, our political system.

sections.label: Commission criteria and deliberative track
sections.summary: Candidates meeting the criteria are passed through by the Commission, while others can use a deliberative track to make their case.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: If you meet those criteria, the Commission is required to then pass you through.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: There is still a deliberative track where candidates who do not automatically qualify can put themselves forward and a case has to be made for why those candidates should be allowed to stand.

sections.label: Existing Presidential Electoral Commission system
sections.summary: Under the existing system, the Presidential Electoral Commission can put forward anyone meeting the criteria, with the public having ultimate scrutiny.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Under the existing system, the Presidential Electoral Commission can put anybody who meets the criteria forward and it is the public then who has ultimate scrutiny over the process.

sections.label: Reserved election for Malay candidate
sections.summary: A direct question asks whether the member supports a reserved election for a Malay candidate or prefers a Malay President with no custodial power.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: A direct question: does he or does he not support the reserved election for a Malay candidate?

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Yes or no, do you support the proposal that there will be a reserved election for a Malay candidate after many decades?

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Or does he prefer for that electoral mandate and for that custodial power that our next Malay President could have, to be removed, and so our next Malay President will be, by his direction, a symbol only with no custodial power?

sections.label: Parliament as initiator, CPA advises
sections.summary: Parliament becomes the initiator, the President does not, the CPA only advises the President, and Parliament makes the legislative decision.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
