sentences.text: Parliament becomes the initiator of the process, and Page: 115 the President does not.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: And the CPA, as proposed, only advises the President.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: And the decision-making – whether it is four, whether it is one extra casting vote, is only about the bar that is then set for Parliament, and ultimately Parliament then has to make the legislative decision.

sections.label: Five-term hiatus and reserved election support
sections.summary: The speaker says they changed their mind on the five-term hiatus and reserved election and fully support the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: But we have to deal with the reality around us, we have to decide if we are going to hold a position as a marker of an ideal for the future, or deal with the reality here and now – deal with what our people face and the issues that we have to help them with.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, on the issue of the five-term hiatus and the reserved election, I have changed my own mind since I first heard about it and I fully support the Bill for all the various reasons that have been described by the Members of this House.

sections.label: Elected Presidency and NCMP changes
sections.summary: The passage says the changes uphold the Constitution, strengthen NCMPs, allow a Malay Elected President and guarantee multiracial representation with a natural sunset.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: It stands in the same vein that we have an Auditor-General and an Attorney-General that does what it has to do to uphold the law, to uphold the best principles of our Constitution and integrity and not to serve a political agenda.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: It strengthens the role of NCMPs and gives voice to people who perhaps have not had a voice before.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: It allows our first Malay Elected President after many decades.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: And it guarantees that we will have an Elected President with representation across all the races.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: And in its mechanism for that multiracial Elected Presidency, it has a natural sunset where, over time, that mechanism may no longer be needed.

sections.label: Constituents' democratic voice in Presidential Election
sections.summary: The passage says constituents voted in the Presidential Election, support the Elected Presidency and will not accept having that democratic voice removed.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Your constituents, the vast majority of all our constituents, whether they voted for the WP or any other Opposition candidate, they voted in the Presidential Election.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: They may have supported different candidates, but they expressed a democratic voice.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: They support the idea of an Elected Presidency and they will not accept having that democratic voice removed.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Could you not demonstrate the ability to change, just as you expect other people to change?

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: I have suggested why the Opposition could vote for the Bill with a clear conscience.

sections.label: President as symbol of national unity
sections.summary: The passage states the President is meant to rise above politics, symbolise national unity, take a long-term view and protect national interest.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: The President is meant to be an office that rises above politics, that acts as a symbol of national unity, that takes a long-term view, and that protects our national interest over and above anything else.

sections.label: Vote for Bill and appointed President proposal
sections.summary: The passage urges voting for the Bill, says a President with under 50% mandate will be seen politically, and suggests an appointed President and elected Senate.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Demonstrate in your actions tomorrow by voting for the Bill to strengthen our system and our country.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: As a result of that process, the Elected President that emerges from there with a mandate that is less than 50% will be seen in a political light and will, therefore, have his or her ability to unify the entire country severely curtailed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: We have suggested returning to an appointed President that can rise above politics and to take the custodial power currently vested in the Elected President and to place it into an elected Senate.

sections.label: Referendum on elected Senate
sections.summary: The passage states Dr Puthucheary said they are rushing to a conclusion on the elected Senate, and they argue for a referendum.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: The second one is that Dr Puthucheary pointed out that we are rushing to a new conclusion about the elected Senate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: We are arguing that the country should go through a referendum on this issue.

sections.label: Appointed body and autocracy claim
sections.summary: The passage says the Member called a Parliament-appointed President an autocrat, and the speaker clarified the autocracy claim concerned a non-elected body.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: The Member made a rather extraordinary statement that a President appointed by Parliament is an autocrat and that amounts to an autocracy.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: If I may begin with your last one, I did not imply that our President would be an autocrat.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: I suggested that the use of an appointed body in the process of the Senatorial Electoral Commission, a non-elected body, to then prevent people arbitrarily from standing for election on a moving target year-on-year ‒ because you have a different pool of candidates ‒ amounted to an autocracy, that you would not then expose the 17th and downstream candidates to the scrutiny of a vote and for the public to make their choice.

sections.label: Custodial powers and candidate numbers
sections.summary: The passage states custodial powers will vest in the President and argues the proposed system limits candidates to 16, making it more politicised and exclusionary.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: The custodial powers that are currently vested in our President will be vested in them.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Under the system currently we are proposing, there is no maximum limit on the number of people who can stand.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: But under your system, it is not that you have come down to 0.2%; you have come down to 16 individuals across the whole of Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: You cannot have a 17th person Page: 120 standing.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, the proposal you have would be more politicised than our current system.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: It will have an increasing dilution of the vote share and it would be increasingly exclusionary because fewer people would potentially be able to stand for elections.

sections.label: Operationalising the Elected Presidency
sections.summary: The passage states the Elected Presidency is settled and that voting a party in a general election does not equate with consenting to it.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: The idea of an Elected Presidency has been settled.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Taking it forward is: how do we operationalise the Elected Presidency?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: There is no simple equation between a GE and a referendum on the issue of the Elected Presidency.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Voting a particular party in a GE does not equate with consenting to the Elected Presidency.

sections.label: Timing of Elected Presidency Bill
sections.summary: The passage asks why the Bill is passed now and states the proposal was not put to the electorate in GE2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: If we are not pressed on this issue, why are we passing this Bill now?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: This proposal of making these changes to the Elected Presidency was not put to the Singapore electorate in GE2015.

sections.label: Risk of polarising direct election
sections.summary: The passage states the speaker does not believe the risk to the Presidency of a polarising direct election has been fundamentally addressed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: The second point, the more important point, I think, is that I do not believe you have fundamentally addressed the issue of the risk to the Presidency of a polarising direct election.

sections.label: President as symbol of unity
sections.summary: The passage states the solution preserves the President as a symbol of unity above politics and that the Constitutional Commission proposed it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: So, our solution is actually so elegant and has such a powerful advantage of preserving the President as a symbol of unity, the unity of the country above politics.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: It is so advantageous in that sense that none less than the Constitutional Commission actually proposed it in its report.

sections.label: Referendum for fundamental issues
sections.summary: The passage states the issue is not whether to have an Elected Presidency and that referendums should be reserved for fundamental issues of sovereignty.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: This was settled long before I came on the scene, but the issue before us is not about whether we have the Elected Presidency.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We have had one referendum: should we merge with Malaysia?

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: A referendum should be reserved for fundamental issues of sovereignty, of the kind of the nation that we want to be.

sections.label: Referendum high bar
sections.summary: Referendums exist in the system with an extraordinarily high bar for the types of things put to the public.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, the issue of whether referendum exists or do not exist, they exist as part of the system.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: There is an extraordinarily high bar set for the types of things that Page: 122 you put forward as a referendum to the public.

sections.label: Public scrutiny and hearings
sections.summary: A general election becomes a proxy for Singaporeans' voice, with extended public scrutiny including nearly a year of hearings and engagements.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: And so, therefore, a GE becomes a proxy for the voice of Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Now, we do not take that absolute approach and, in between a proposal or a discussion, we have an extended period of public scrutiny and public session, which is exactly what we have done – nearly a year of public hearings, a Constitutional Commission, debate in print, debate in person, engagements.

sections.label: Proposals not sent to Commission
sections.summary: The proposals were not submitted to the Constitutional Commission, where independent legal experts could have examined them.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: You have not submitted this to the Constitutional Commission where you would have had independent legal experts and all the various minds that applied themselves to this series of problems that you have highlighted to examine your proposals.

sections.label: Senate proposal and Presidency
sections.summary: The Senate proposal is said to save the Presidency from politicisation, letting it rise above politics as a non-political unifying symbol.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: You are saying our Senate proposal is just as bad because the senatorial election could be politicised, just like the Presidential Election.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: But you have not addressed the elephant in the room, which is that our proposal saves the Presidency from politicisation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: It allows the Presidency to rise above politics and be a unifying force, that one symbol that is non-political, unlike Dr Janil Puthucheary, unlike myself, that one symbol that is not political.

sections.label: Saving Presidency false argument
sections.summary: Saving the Presidency is called a false argument because the proposed Presidency differs fundamentally, losing its custodial role and electoral mandate.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: The issue of saving the Presidency is a false argument because the Presidency that you are proposing is a fundamentally different Presidency from what we have today and what we are proposing in the future.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, you are saving the Presidency by removing the opportunity for an electoral mandate because he or she will no longer have a custodial role.

sections.label: Symbolic Presidency and Senate
sections.summary: The position described supports a symbolic Presidency with custodial powers and the electoral process devolved to a Senate.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: If I can understand your position, you are supporting very much a symbolic Presidency with a devolution of all the custodial powers and, Page: 124 hence, the electoral process to a Senate, the eligibility criteria of which would be an approximate to the eligibility criteria of our current President and there will be an exclusionary process at 16, where you feel that somehow this is better than our current system.

sections.label: Expanded CPA and Elected President
sections.summary: The CPA expands to eight members and the Elected President must consult it on monetary matters and key appointments, making it the key decision-maker.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: The CPA will be expanded to eight members and the Elected President is now obliged to consult the CPA on all monetary matters related to the Reserves and all key Public Service appointments.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: With the expanded powers, and the system of strong and weak vetoes by the Elected President depending on how the CPA votes, the CPA has become the key decision-maker.

sections.label: CPA as third key
sections.summary: Opening the Reserves requires the Elected President's agreement or the CPA's agreement, so the CPA has become a third key.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: In order to open the locked box of Reserves, the Government would need either the Elected President's agreement, or failing which, the CPA's agreement.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: The CPA has effectively become a third key.

sections.label: CPA member qualifications
sections.summary: Eligibility criteria for the Elected Presidency are tightened, but nothing ensures CPA members have the expertise and experience for their powerful vote.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: However, similar qualifications are not applied to the appointment of CPA members, save for general precepts such as those requiring a member to be of "integrity, good character and reputation", as mentioned in the White Paper.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: So, while the eligibility criteria for the Elected Presidency will be tightened significantly so as to narrow the field of candidates down to a select super elite few in society, nothing is being done to ensure that the CPA members will have the right expertise and experience to exercise their powerful vote to swing crucial decisions of state.

sections.label: CPA as centre of power
sections.summary: The CPA, like the Cabinet, has become a potential centre of power, a third key, with two more members and expanded scope.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: On the other hand, the analogy is correct in that the CPA, like the Cabinet, appears to have become another potential centre of power, a third key, with the weight of its collective judgement strengthened with the addition of two more members and scope expanded to all monetary matters concerning the Reserves and all key appointments.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: The CPA is already politicised, knowing that its decision would swing the veto, knowing that the collective judgement of six and now eight wise Page: 126 men in CPA would carry much weight in the court of public opinion, knowing that any dissenting views disclosed and published would affect political debate, calculating that any check on the President's veto would require a two-third majority to override.

sections.label: Elections for CPA members
sections.summary: The passage asks why the CPA, as a third key making political decisions, should not be made accountable through list elections.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: Since the CPA has become a third key making political decisions, why not make it accountable to the people and give the CPA its proper political mandate by holding list elections for the CPA members – become a Senate?

sections.label: Senate and two-key system
sections.summary: The Presidency would be indirectly elected by Parliament, and the elected CPA, called the Senate, would hold the second key.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: Return the Presidency to being the dignified ceremonial Head of State again, to be indirectly elected by Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: The elected CPA, let us call it the Senate, will then hold the second key in a direct relationship to Parliament in a truly two-key system of deliberation, veto and override that is transparent and accountable.

sections.label: Elected Senate proposal criticised
sections.summary: The speaker says the elected Senate proposal is flawed in substance and process and does not address objections raised against the Elected Presidency.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: I will focus my speech on the proposal that has been put forward for an elected Senate.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: This proposal is fundamentally flawed – flawed in substance and flawed in terms of the process.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Their proposal for an elected Senate does not deal with any of the objections they have raised for the Elected Presidency.

sections.label: Senate candidates qualifications
sections.summary: The WP position paper objects to a super elite narrowing candidates, yet the Senate proposal has eight people with Elected President qualifications.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: In their position paper, the WP talks about the objection in terms of this being restricted to "a super elite" and it narrows the field of candidates.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: But then, if you look at the Senate proposal, it is to have eight such people where the same qualifications as an Elected President should have.

sections.label: Eight Elected Presidents
sections.summary: The speaker says Senators would meet the same criteria as Elected Presidents, so instead of one there would be eight.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: He went further to say that the criteria are the same as set out in the Bill that is before Parliament, meaning, I suppose, in context, Senators should meet the criteria proposed for Elected Presidents.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: So, instead of one Elected President, we would have eight Elected Presidents.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Does it not make the position eight times worse?

sections.label: Small pool objection
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the Senate proposal makes the WP's objection about a small establishment candidate pool eight times worse.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The second major objection that the WP has made is that the candidates will be drawn from a small pool, likely to be establishment and the whole purpose of this exercise and the whole purpose of the exercise over the last 25 years, is to fix a non-PAP Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But if that was the fear, does not the Senate proposal make the position eight times worse?

sections.label: Election mandate objection
sections.summary: The speaker quotes the position paper saying popular election tempts a candidate to claim a mandate beyond constitutional powers, and asks how eight Presidents help.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Your position paper says the competitive election process pits individuals against one another and the outcomes of a popular election, I quote, "tempts… the elected candidate to claim a mandate beyond his or her constitutional powers." So, how do eight Presidents in a Senate help?

sections.label: Senatorial Election Committee selection
sections.summary: The speaker describes the suggestion that a Senatorial Election Committee will select 16 even if there are 17 or 20 equal candidates.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Second, on the selection process, an extraordinary suggestion on selection – that there will be a Senatorial Election Committee (SEC) which will select 16, even if you have 17 or 20 candidates of equal quality.

sections.label: Casting vote and nine Senators
sections.summary: A question is asked about who would hold the casting vote, noting a proposal of nine Senators rather than eight.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If so, who will have that casting vote?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: He also said that we could have nine Senators – so, nine rather than eight.

sections.label: Senator criteria same as President
sections.summary: Mr Leon Perera and Mr Dennis Tan said Senator criteria match those for the Elected President, but only after a long detour.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Leon Perera and Mr Dennis Tan said the criteria for the Senators are the same as for the Elected President, but only after a long detour.

sections.label: WP position and Senate proposal
sections.summary: The WP took a position before the Constitutional Commission on parliamentary super majority for Reserves, and now an Upper House Senate is suggested.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The WP took one position before the Constitutional Commission.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Parliamentary super majority if Government wants to touch the Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Now, the suggestion is of an Upper House – Senate.

sections.label: Goh quote on Elected Presidency
sections.summary: An unquoted second part of a statement by Prime Minister Goh about the Elected Presidency is cited.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The second part which he did not quote was this: "Dishonest men who aspire for power will, I believe, never propose this Bill." Prime Minister Goh was talking about the Elected Presidency.

sections.label: CPA swing vote contradiction
sections.summary: The unelected CPA having the swing vote between the Elected President and Parliament is called a contradiction, prompting a question to the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: The contradiction is the unelected CPA having the swing vote to decide between the Elected President and Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: So, Mdm Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister this: i the President needs to be elected to have this democratic mandate to say "no" to Parliament, which is your view, what mandate does the CPA have to influence legislature and say "yes" or "no" to an Elected President and to Parliament?

sections.label: WP proposal to abolish Elected President
sections.summary: The WP proposes abolishing the Elected President and restoring the ceremonial role, citing the President's dual role and tensions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: First, I am flattered that he has spent so much time to try to cross-examine the WP on details which he said, "don't gel" and so on.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But one of the things which I think he and also the Government have not addressed, which we have put forth as one of the weaknesses that the Government proposal or existing process is, is the current expectation of the Government for the President to play the dual role of being a custodian as well as being a Head of State.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Minister has acknowledged there are inherent tensions, and the Constitutional Commission had also received evidence and thought it necessary to record that.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: So, our proposal really for the abolition of the Elected President and the restoration of the ceremonial role of the President would protect the President from having this potential need to confront the Government and now even confront an expanded and stronger CPA.

sections.label: Reserved election for Malay candidate
sections.summary: The passage states the next election will be reserved for a Malay candidate and that the system's design and potential problems are not being discussed.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: We are not talking about the design of the system and what potential problems it could have.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: And the next election is going to be reserved for a Malay candidate".

sections.label: Inherent tensions in President's roles
sections.summary: It acknowledges inherent tensions in the President's dual roles but rejects neutering the Presidency or replacing it with a fundamentally flawed institution.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: As to the current expectation on the inherent tensions, yes, there are inherent tensions between having a President performing both roles, but you do not deal with that by suggesting that you neuter the Presidency, do away with the institution and put forward another institution which is fundamentally flawed, both in substance and in process, and then say, "Here, we have a proposal".

sections.label: Current solution until better one
sections.summary: It states that one cannot say it can never happen, but until a better solution exists, this is the solution.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: One does not say therefore that it can never happen.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But until there is a better solution, this is the solution we have.

sections.label: Constitutional Commission recommendations on Elected Presidency
sections.summary: The Constitutional Commission made recommendations on the Elected Presidency, most being implemented, and later observed another process the Government could consider.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Constitutional Commission made its recommendations on the Elected Presidency, most of which are being implemented now.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They made a further observation subsequently about another process that the Government could consider.

sections.label: Goh Chok Tong on mixed Senate
sections.summary: On 5 October 1990, then-Deputy Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said the Government was creating a mixed Senate of six appointed and one elected Senator.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: On 5 October 1990, then-Deputy Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said that what essentially was happening was that the Government was creating a mixed Senate: six appointed Senators forming the Council, and one elected Senator that would be the Elected President.

sections.label: Government considered elected Upper House
sections.summary: Previous White Papers show the Government carefully considered a Senate, but its approach differed and it has explained an elected Upper House is inherently unworkable.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: You can also look at the previous White Papers and they tell you and show you that the Government considered the question of a Senate, an Upper House, very carefully.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But the Government's approach to a Senate was very different from the approach that you are proposing, which, fundamentally, is unworkable.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Government has explained that an elected Upper House is inherently unworkable and has explained it many times why.

sections.label: Custodian risk to Reserves
sections.summary: The speaker says the risk of a custodian raiding the Reserves is a bigger risk worth taking until a better system is suggested.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We do not run away from the problem.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But when you balance out, ultimately, the requirement for a custodian to safeguard the Reserves from dishonest people who will want to raid the Reserves, it is a bigger risk.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: You need to deal with that bigger risk.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And until and unless someone can suggest a better system, our assessment is that this is a risk worth taking.

sections.label: Elected President versus Senate
sections.summary: The speaker notes a position paper called one elected President elitist and narrow, yet wanted 16 similarly qualified Senate candidates with eight elected.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In your position paper, you say, on the election of one elected President, that it is super elitist and it is such a narrow criterion and so on.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But then you turned around and you said, you want 16 people with the same qualifications to run for the Senate, of whom eight will be elected.

sections.label: Constitutional Commission recommendations
sections.summary: The speaker says the Constitutional Commission gave relevant recommendations and added an observation for the Government to consider.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Faisal Manap, one does not have to characterise the Constitutional Commission's proposals.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: What I will say is that the Constitutional Commission gave many important recommendations which were directly relevant to the questions that were asked.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In addition, it added an observation for the Government to consider if it wished and if it wanted to accept.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: That is what the Commission said, and I think we will keep to the Commission's words.

sections.label: President and $500 million criterion
sections.summary: The speaker says the President ensures wise Reserve spending, and the $500 million shareholders' equity criterion is not exclusionary, so a chief financial officer could qualify.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: The President, as an institution, will play an important role to ensure that the government of the day displays wisdom when it comes to spending the Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: There has been feedback from the public about how the bar or threshold has been set too high for candidates, that a person's firm must have a minimum of $500 million in shareholders' equity, which means that only the most senior executives of large, complex companies are eligible, further reducing the available pool of talent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: As mentioned by Deputy Prime Minister Teo yesterday, this $500 million criterion is not an exclusion criterion and one does not need to be the most senior executive in a large company.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Therefore, even a chief financial officer could qualify as a candidate, for instance, as he/she would understand numbers, good governance and what it takes to safeguard national Reserves.

sections.label: Council consultation and appointments
sections.summary: The speaker supports obliging the President to consult the Council on fiscal matters and key appointments, and adding two Council members.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: We have seen how misdeeds are sometimes uncovered years after a person has left an organisation or company, or perhaps due to a whistleblower in that organisation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: I support the changes made to the Bill whereby the President should be obliged to consult the Council before exercising his discretion in respect of all fiscal matters touching on Singapore's Reserves and all matters regarding key public appointments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: I also support the changes to augment the Council with two additional members, one appointed by the President and the other by the Prime Minister.

sections.label: Multiracial Presidency safeguard mechanism
sections.summary: The speaker supports a hiatus-triggered safeguard for multiracial representation in the Presidency without undermining meritocracy, but worries minority candidates may be insufficient.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: My second point is that I support the changes to the Bill to ensure multiracial representation in the Presidency via a hiatus-triggered safeguard mechanism without undermining meritocracy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: I am also confident that this pool will become bigger in the future since many Malays are doing well academically, received Government scholarships and are currently enjoying success in many fields.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: However, one of my concerns is that there may not be sufficient minority candidates when needed.

sections.label: Reserves check outside Parliament
sections.summary: Singapore's good Reserve requires an institution outside Parliament to check Reserve spending and restrain spending where necessary.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Singapore has built up a good Reserve, and so there is a need for an institution outside of Parliament to check on the spending of Reserves and restrain spending where necessary.

sections.label: EP role not everything
sections.summary: The public should note the Elected President's role is not to check and balance everything, as past candidates misled voters.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: All said, it is pertinent for the public to note that the EP's role is not to provide checks and balances on anything and everything, just as how candidates in the previous elections have misled voters into believing so.

sections.label: Changes and eight-member Senate
sections.summary: The changes aim to build a society where Singaporeans are not marginalised, and an eight-member Senate was suggested.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: While these may seem unimaginable in peaceful, harmonious Singapore, we cannot guarantee that it would not lead to an earthquake when the fissures start to surface.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: It is hoped that these latest changes can step up the efforts to create a society in which all Singaporeans know that they will not be marginalised or shut out, that they truly have a place to call Singapore their home and their own country.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: They have suggested the formation of an eight-member Senate.

sections.label: Sylvia Lim on CPA
sections.summary: Ms Sylvia Lim says it is really no change from the existing CPA.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim says it is really no change from the existing CPA.

sections.label: Malay President reserved election
sections.summary: Singapore has not had a Malay President in 46 years, and next year's election will be reserved for Malays.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: But it is our principle to consult and discuss openly about such issues in Singapore, especially since our community has become more mature.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: It is true that for 46 years, Singapore has not had a Malay President since Encik Yusof Ishak.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: So, we should be heartened that this was considered, especially with the announcement that next year's election will be reserved for Malays.

sections.label: Five terms about 25 years
sections.summary: The recommended five terms is about 25 years, and the proposal takes effect only if no minority President is elected in that time.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Thirdly, the recommended period of five terms is a very long time, that is, about 25 years.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: And if there are no Presidents from the minority groups within these 25 years, only then will this new proposal take effect.

sections.label: CNA-IPS survey on race voting
sections.summary: A 2016 CNA-IPS survey found Singaporeans comfortable living with other races but inclined to vote for a President and Prime Minister of their own race.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In the Channel NewsAsia-Institute of Policy Studies (CNA-IPS) survey in 2016, Singaporeans are found to be comfortable interacting and living together with the other communities and other races.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: But when the time comes to vote, they are more inclined to elect a President and Prime Minister from their own race.

sections.label: Racial Discrimination Convention signing
sections.summary: Singapore signed the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination in 2015 and will ratify it in 2017.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Another issue, Madam, is with regard to the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination that Singapore signed in 2015 and will ratify in 2017, whereby this matter was also highlighted.

sections.label: US female President example
sections.summary: The United States has never had a female President in 240 years, with Hillary Clinton a candidate at present.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: If we look at, for instance, the United States (US) – a First World and progressive nation – 240 years have passed but they have never had a female President until the present time, whereby Hillary Clinton is a candidate.

sections.label: Race preference for President
sections.summary: A candidate's race should be irrelevant in a meritocratic society, but the CNA-IPS survey found many Singaporeans still prefer a President of their own race.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: After all, the racial group of a qualified candidate should be irrelevant in our meritocratic and race-blind society.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: However, the reality is that we are not quite a race-blind society, as the CNA-IPS survey had found.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: A significant proportion of Singaporeans would still prefer a President to be of their own race.

sections.label: Malay President and inclusivity
sections.summary: Singapore has had no Malay President or candidate since the Elected Presidency began in 1991, and the next Elected President will be from the Malay community.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: It is important to acknowledge the need to be more inclusive of our minorities and ensure that they feel that they are also an integral part of our community.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: We have not had a Malay President or even a Malay candidate since the Elected Presidency commenced in 1991.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Our only Malay President, the late Mr Yusof Ishak, was appointed after our Independence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: I am, therefore, very happy to note that our next Elected President will be from the Malay community.

sections.label: Reserved election for Eurasian President
sections.summary: The speaker hopes it would be ideal to ensure reserved elections for a Eurasian Elected President.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: By bringing something different to the table, we can help enrich the office of the Elected Presidency.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Hence, I hope it would be ideal to ensure reserved elections for a Eurasian Elected President.

sections.label: Inter-ethnic marriages proportion
sections.summary: The proportion of inter-ethnic marriages has almost doubled from a decade ago, with 21.5% of marriages last year being inter-ethnic.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: The proportion of inter-ethnic marriages has almost doubled from a decade ago.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: Last year, 21.5% of marriages were inter-ethnic marriages.

sections.label: Multiracialism safeguards in Singapore
sections.summary: Singapore established the Presidential Council for Minority Rights in 1970, the GRC system in 1988, and the Ethnic Integration Policy in 1989 to safeguard multiracialism.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: In 1970, the Presidential Council for Minority Rights was established to examine all legislation to ensure that they are not disadvantageous to any racial or religious community as compared to other such communities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: Since 1988, our society's multiracialism has been safeguarded in our Parliamentary system through the GRC system, where at least one of the MPs must belong to one of the minority racial communities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: The Ethnic Integration Policy, which was introduced in March 1989, aims to ensure a balanced racial mix in every neighbourhood and block which approximates the general population.

sections.label: Comfort in choosing similar
sections.summary: The speaker attributes choices of similar persons to comfort and convenience, not deep prejudice, citing 59% of Chinese accepting a Malay President and 75% of Malays accepting an Indian President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: I do not believe that this is from a sense of deep prejudice or bigotry than a sense of comfort and convenience to choose someone similar to yourself.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: This is apparent when, based on the same findings, 59% of Chinese would still say yes to a Malay President, while 75% of Malays would still say "yes" to an Indian President.

sections.label: Reserved Presidential Election proposal
sections.summary: The speaker is glad that a proposed change to the Elected Presidency is a reserved Presidential Election for a racial group.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: Indeed, just because we have learnt to live with our differences and can cherish them, does not mean the differences do not matter or the differences have disappeared.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: So, I am glad that one of the proposed changes that will be introduced to the Elected Presidency is to have a reserved Presidential Election for a racial group.

sections.label: Sri Lankan language policy effects
sections.summary: Sri Lanka's 1944 policy making Sinhalese the sole official language excluded Tamil-speaking minorities, and the 1981 Jaffna Library burning likely triggered 26 years of civil war.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: One policy of the Sri Lankan government in 1944 making Sinhalese the sole official language, excluded Tamil-speaking minorities from the civil service and limited entry into universities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: The burning down of the Jaffna Library in 1981 was probably the ultimate trigger of 26 years of "bombs, bullets, carnage and suffering" from the civil war.

sections.label: Constitutional amendment for minority Presidents
sections.summary: The Constitution was amended to ensure a candidate from each race can become an Elected President, changing a situation not conducive for minority candidates.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: The amendment to the Constitution to ensure that a candidate from each race can become an Elected President is another adjustment that was made this time round to change a situation that has not been conducive for someone from the minority group to become President.

sections.label: Foreign fighter estimate 2015
sections.summary: The Soufan Group estimates 27,000 foreign fighters at the end of 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: The Soufan Group estimates 27,000 foreign fighters at the end of 2015.

sections.label: Singapore terrorism arrests
sections.summary: Singapore arrested a dozen self-radicalised Singaporeans, some intending to join ISIS in the Middle East and a few planning attacks in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: Even Singapore is not immune to the growing threat of terrorism.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: The Government has arrested a dozen Singaporeans, most of whom were self-radicalised.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: Several intended to go to the Middle East to join ISIS, and a few were planning to mount attacks in Singapore.

sections.label: Constitutional amendment for Elected President
sections.summary: The Constitution was amended to ensure all ethnic groups a chance at becoming an Elected President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: The amendment of the Constitution to ensure all ethnic groups a chance at becoming an Elected President will be remembered as a prudent foresight of the Government and a great generosity of the majority.

sections.label: Cameroon migrant voting for empathy
sections.summary: A Cameroon-born US citizen described American empathy and kindness, and said she would vote for empathy on Election Day.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: She migrated from Cameroon and became an US citizen years ago.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: And she wrote, "I've seen the best of America during my time here.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: When I was considering dropping out of graduate school because of financial constraints, an American professor helped me get a scholarship so I could complete my master's degree.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: Twice, I had an American co-worker give me hand-me-downs because I couldn't afford to buy clothes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: An American employer once said to me, at a time when I was questioning who I was, 'You are a breath of fresh air'.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: But the empathy Americans have shown me far outweighs the unkindness.

sentences.speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
sentences.text: That is why on Election Day, I'll be voting for empathy." Yesterday, too, I felt a poignant moment when the Prime Minister said, "As Minister Yaacob Ibrahim observed yesterday, this would be our first Malay Elected President after more than 46 years, since our first President Encik Yusof Ishak." And the Prime Minister finished with, "I look forward to this." There was spontaneous applause from my colleagues – Chinese and minorities alike.

sections.label: Eligible Malay Singaporeans for President
sections.summary: An MP asked how many Malay Singaporeans would be eligible to run for President under the amended eligibility criteria.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Based on the proposed amendments and the Prime Minister's earlier announcement, Madam, I would like to ask how many Malay Singaporeans would be eligible to run for President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Do we have a rough estimate based on the amended eligibility criteria?

sections.label: Reserved elections and Bukit Batok
sections.summary: The passage says reserved elections allow this, and cites Mr Murali Pillai's Bukit Batok by-election win as showing race may not be an important factor.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Having reserved elections allows us to do this, though it may appear to be affirmative action or betray a belief that minority candidates are not capable of being elected on their own merits or that our electorate still largely votes along racial lines.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The fact that Mr Murali Pillai won a resounding victory in the recent Bukit Batok by-election perhaps serves as a useful test case, which shows that race may not be such an important factor.

sections.label: Survey on racist attitudes
sections.summary: A survey found 45% heard racist comments at work, 27% accept race-based hiring refusal, and few Chinese Singaporeans would accept Malay or Indian managers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The recent survey indicates that 45% of respondents have heard racist comments in their workplace; 27% think it is okay not to hire someone because of his or her race; and only 35% and 41% of Chinese Singaporeans said they would accept a Malay or Indian Singaporean respectively to manage their businesses.

sections.label: Vote for non-establishment candidate
sections.summary: Many Singaporeans wanted a non-establishment alternative voice, explaining Mr Chua Kim Yeow's 41.3% national vote despite being unknown and barely campaigning.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: There was a palpable sense that many Singaporeans wanted to elect a non-establishment candidate to provide an alternative voice and to balance a one-party dominant system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: That explains why the late Mr Chua Kim Yeow obtained 41.3% of the vote – the national vote, mind you – although he was relatively unknown and hardly campaigned at all.

sections.label: Menon Commission appointed President proposal
sections.summary: The Menon Commission suggested an appointed President with a symbolic role, rotated among ethnic groups, but the Government rejected this advice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: They had the courage to do so and suggested that we cast our eyes back to the time when Presidents were not elected.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: And I quote from their report, "The President would retain his symbolic and ceremonial role of the Head of State as it had been at independence and hold an appointed office.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Parliament would abide by the convention by rotating the office among the different ethnic groups." Madam, they are right.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Yet, the Government has rejected the Menon Commission's advice on this hugely important issue, which is the nub of this debate.

sections.label: WP appointed President Malay outcome
sections.summary: Under the WP's proposal for an appointed President, a Malay President would have come long before now.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Under the WP's proposal for an appointed President, we would have had a Malay President a long time before now.

sections.label: Paid-up capital threshold raised
sections.summary: The Bill replaces the $100 million automatic inclusion threshold with $500 million, raising the bar despite a deliberative track.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: As for updating the paid-up capital requirements, this Bill replaces a $100 million threshold for automatic inclusion with a $500 million one.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: There is a deliberative track, yes, but the bar for automatic inclusion is now raised.

sections.label: Changes prevent non-establishment candidate
sections.summary: Eligible candidates decreased from 2016 despite Government claims, suggesting changes aim to prevent a non-establishment candidate becoming President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: The Government has said that the number of eligible candidates would not decrease versus the number in 1992.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: The number of eligible candidates has decreased from the number in 2016.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Taken all together, Mdm Speaker, it is hard to resist the conclusion that the Government is making these changes to prevent an alternative, non-establishment sanctioned candidate from becoming the next President of Singapore.

sections.label: NCMPs and grassroots resources
sections.summary: NCMPs cannot use public facilities or PA resources for grassroots activities in contested wards, likely capping Opposition presence at 12.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: NCMPs cannot use public facilities or draw on the People's Association's (PA) lavish resources to fund grassroots activities in the wards they contested, as my colleague, Mr Dennis Tan, observed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: The likely effect of this is to cap Opposition presence in this Chamber at 12, but more importantly, much more importantly, if this scheme is fully exploited by the Ruling Party and fully embraced by voters in the way that the PAP hopes, it would be 12 unelectable Opposition MPs, and that is a crucial difference.

sections.label: Population and infrastructure mismatch
sections.summary: It asks what happens if population and infrastructure mismatch again, as in the 2000s when trains, hospitals and housing were stressed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: What if we get another mismatch between population and infrastructure, such as what happened during the decade of the 2000s, when our trains, hospitals and housing stock were severely stressed and Singaporeans suffered, necessitating policy reversals after the GE of 2011 to repair the damage?

sections.label: Media reform and NCMP scheme
sections.summary: It calls for regulated but free competition in broadsheet newspapers, television and radio, and asks if the goal is 100% of elected seats.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Reform the regulation of the media to allow for regulated but free competition in broadsheet newspapers, television and radio.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: With this amendment to the NCMP scheme, is it your goal that your party wins 100% of elected seats in Parliament?

sections.label: Eligibility criteria for private-sector candidates
sections.summary: It states no eligibility criteria list will satisfy everyone, but changing criteria for private-sector candidates is timely given two decades of economic change.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: There will never be a list of specific eligibility criteria that everyone will agree on.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: However, I believe that the overall recommendation to change the eligibility criteria for candidates from the private sector is timely and appropriate, especially when we consider how the economic and business environment has changed in the last two decades.

sections.label: Constitutionally reserved Elected President
sections.summary: The Bill will enshrine in the Constitution a guaranteed Elected President from a particular ethnic group via a closed-election system reserved for that group.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: What is new, however, is that this Bill, for the first time, will enshrine in our Constitution that Singapore is guaranteed to have an Elected President from a particular ethnic group from time to time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: This will be done via a proposed "closed-election" system reserved for that particular ethnic group, should there be no president from that group after a certain period.

sections.label: Rise in interracial marriages
sections.summary: SingStats figures show interracial marriages rose from about 7.6% of all marriages in 1990 to about 21.5% in 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: If I may reference Minister Masagos, the statistics that were published by SingStats indicate that the number of interracial marriages is on the rise, from approximately 7.6% of all total marriages in 1990, to about 21.5% of all marriages in 2015.

sections.label: Preference for own ethnic leaders
sections.summary: More than 85% of respondents preferred national leaders from their own ethnic group.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: More than 85% of respondents indicated a preference for national leaders from their own ethnic group.

sections.label: Race in political elections
sections.summary: The speaker says harmony and tolerance may not translate to race-blind elections, as race remains significant in the sociopolitical sphere.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: But based on this, I feel that while Singaporeans might be accepting of other ethnic groups in terms of their cultures and traditions and that we all live in peace and harmony, this harmony and tolerance might not translate to truly "race-blind" political elections.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: This is a sobering reality that we have to face and acknowledge that race continues to be a significant factor in our sociopolitical sphere.

sections.label: Closed-election for ethnic representation
sections.summary: The speaker says going years without an Elected President from an ethnic group is undesirable, and a closed-election is not tokenism or a compromise on equality and meritocracy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Going for many years without an Elected President from a particular ethnic group is certainly not desirable and does not reflect the multiracial and multicultural spirit of our country.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: A circuit breaker "closed-election" that ensures that an eligible and qualified president from a particular ethnic group is elected from time to time is not merely tokenism or "affirmative action"; neither is it a compromise on the values of equality and meritocracy.

sections.label: Never known a Malay President
sections.summary: The speaker says he and his generation have never known a Malay President, and hopes this changes in 2017 if the Bill passes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: In the course of my lifetime, and many of my generation, and the generation that has come after me, we have never known a Malay President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I am heartened, however, that should this Bill get passed, and should an eligible candidate step forward that next year, this will change and I can then put my hand on heart and say that I am proud to have known a Malay Singaporean as my Elected President in my lifetime and it is something that not just me, or my generation but all Singaporeans should be proud of come 2017.

sections.label: Reserving Presidency for racial group
sections.summary: The speaker cites a system based on justice and equality, and the Bill's amendment reserving the Elected Presidency for a racial group unrepresented for five terms.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: We do this through a system that is "based on justice and equality".

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This brings me to the Bill's amendment of reserving the Elected Presidency for a racial group if it is not represented for five terms.

sections.label: Mechanism honouring justice and equality
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the proposed mechanism in the amendment Bill honours the vision of justice and equality.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Yet, while racial representation is valued, how we achieve it is equally important.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, my question is: does the proposed mechanism in the amendment Bill honour the vision of justice and equality that we aspire towards?

sections.label: Young Malay Singaporeans on selection
sections.summary: Young Malay Singaporeans would welcome a Malay President but questioned the selection process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: If so, then having this provision may not eradicate the problem but, in fact, indicates that there is a lot of work to be done to achieve our vision.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I have spoken to a number of young Malay Singaporeans and, while most agreed that they would welcome and be proud to have a Malay President, they questioned the process of the selection.

sections.label: Minority representation amendment concerns
sections.summary: The provision may let the majority argue it already allows minority Presidents, negating real outreach.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The fact that we need to amend the Elected Presidency Bill to ensure minority representation says a lot about how far the majority is from real engagement with minority races.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In fact, such a provision may exacerbate the issue, in that it provides a convenient argument for the majority to say this special provision already allows for a Malay, Indian or Eurasian President, negating the need to really reach out, understand, appreciate and support the best candidate, regardless of race, language or religion.

sections.label: CNA-IPS survey on race relations
sections.summary: A survey found most Singaporeans heard racist comments, often from colleagues and friends, and many ignored them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: According to a survey on race relations commissioned by CNA-IPS, nearly two in three Singaporeans surveyed have heard racist comments being made, and about half the time, it was by workplace colleagues and friends.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Faced with such comments, 65% of respondents said they ignored the person's comments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This is in spite of the fact that 84% said they would get upset if they heard racist comments about any race; 62% said it was never acceptable to make jokes about another race in the company of friends; and 67% said it was never acceptable to call a racial group terms like dirty, lazy or money-minded.

sections.label: Reserved Presidential election amendment
sections.summary: The Bill reserves the next Presidential election for a racial group absent from the office for five terms.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As proposed by this amendment Bill, when a member from any racial group has not occupied the President's office after five continuous terms, the next Presidential election will be reserved for a candidate from that racial group.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: By proposing this amendment, the Government is reminding us that many people vote along racial lines.

sections.label: Presidential nominee qualifications reminder
sections.summary: The speaker reminds the House that a Presidential nominee's qualifications may be important.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In view of this, I would, therefore, like to remind the House of this: yes, it may be important for the Presidential nominee to have qualifications, such as having being a chief executive officer (CEO) of a company of more than S$500 million of shareholders' equity or having been in senior positions in the Public Service.

sections.label: Ombudsman in Office of President
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether an ombudsman role of mediation could reside in the Office of the President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As articulated very fluently by my fellow Nominated Parliamentarian Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, we are faced with a complex world rife with standoffs and contestations among people, the government, interest groups and so on.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: There were indications in the 2011 Presidential Election that Singaporeans yearn for alternative possibilities to deal with such difficult situations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Some had hoped that the Elected President could provide such an alternative institution for arbitration or maybe for mediation, something akin to what Prof Tommy Koh and President Tony Tan have suggested: an ombudsman.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Could this ombudsman, a role of mediation and negotiation, and one built on trust, reside in the Office of the President, given that it possesses a unifying symbol for the nation?

sections.label: President moral integrity and fair election
sections.summary: The passage states crises test the President's moral integrity and independence, and that the President must be elected by a fair system upholding equality and justice regardless of race, language, religion, class, gender or sexual orientation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is in crises that the true mantle of the President is tested, where his or her moral integrity and independence is counted upon to make necessary decisions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: We must, therefore, ensure that the President is elected based on a fair system, one that embraces the values of equality and justice that we seek to uphold, regardless of race, language or religion; regardless or class, gender or sexual orientation.

sections.label: Reserved Presidential Election Malay joy
sections.summary: The passage states that when the Prime Minister announced the upcoming Presidential Elections would be reserved for Malays, there was joy in the community.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Yesterday, when the Prime Minister announced that the upcoming Presidential Elections will be reserved for Malays, there was a feeling of joy in our community.

sections.label: Constitutional Commission report and discussions
sections.summary: The passage states an independent Constitutional Commission's review produced a 153-page report excluding annexes, and that after the Government's White Paper the speaker held discussions with many Singaporeans personally and as an MP.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Following the Prime Minister's announcement, an independent Constitutional Commission conducted a thorough review which culminated in a 153-page report, excluding the annexes.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: In the wake of the Government's White Paper in response to the Constitutional Commission report, I engaged in numerous discussions with many Singaporeans on the issue; in my personal capacity and as a Member of Parliament.

sections.label: Reserved election against Singaporean values
sections.summary: The passage states that in the discussions, some felt the proposal for a reserved election for a certain race ran against the grain of Singaporean values.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: With regard to my first point, in the discussions, some felt that the proposal to ensure a reserved election for a certain race ran against the grain of our Singaporean values.

sections.label: Others see pragmatic step forward
sections.summary: The passage states that others felt the proposal is a pragmatic step forward.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: On the other hand, others felt that this is a pragmatic step forward.

sections.label: Malay reserved election excitement buzz
sections.summary: The passage states that when the Prime Minister announced the next Presidential Election would be reserved for the Malay community, there was a buzz of excitement among many in the community.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: When the Prime Minister announced yesterday that the next Presidential Election would be reserved for the Malay community, there was a buzz of excitement among many in the community.

sections.label: Minority representation in Presidency
sections.summary: The speaker supports the Bill, saying it addresses minority representation in the Elected President's office and promotes multiracialism with minimum intervention.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Despite my earlier reservations, I am fully supportive of this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: In particular, I believe there is an important need to address the issue of minority representation in the office of the President.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I believe that the changes put forth address these needs and promote multiracialism by introducing a concept of racial representation in the Elected President's office.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: The proposed Bill reflects minimum intervention and does no more than necessary to achieve the aim of ensuring that all racial groups are represented in the Presidency.

sections.label: President sharing power with CPA
sections.summary: The Bill requires the Elected President to share power with an enlarged CPA and consult it on fiscal matters touching the Reserves and key Public Service appointments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: With the passing of this amendment Bill, the Elected President will have to share power with an enlarged CPA in the discharge of his custodial and key appointment roles.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: The CPA, although only an appointed body, is bestowed with considerable powers to challenge and delay the decision of the President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: This Bill also imposes a general duty on the President to consult the CPA before exercising his discretion in respect of all fiscal matters touching on the Reserves and all matters relating to key Public Service appointments.

sections.label: CPA member appointments and terms
sections.summary: The Prime Minister and President each appoint three CPA members over three staggered terms, with two tie-breaker appointments from the Chief Justice and Public Service Commission Chairman.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: The Prime Minister and President can appoint three members to the CPA each, evenly spread over three staggered terms, the remaining two of the tie-breaker appointments will come from the Chief Justice and Chairman of the Public Service Commission respectively.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: The President will not be able to appoint his first member to the CPA until 2020.

sections.label: Chua's share of votes
sections.summary: Mr Chua received 41.31% of the total votes cast.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: Mr Chua got a very respectable 41.31% of the total votes cast.

sections.label: Tony Tan's election margin
sections.summary: President Tony Tan was elected with 35.2% of valid votes, beating Dr Tan Cheng Bock by 0.35%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: The nation was so divided that President Tony Tan was elected on a mandate of 35.2% of the valid votes, beating Dr Tan Cheng Bock by a margin of 0.35%.

sections.label: Narrowing eligible presidential candidates
sections.summary: The speaker says the changes will narrow the pool of eligible presidential candidates, though the Minister said they are not targeted at any individual.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: So, the next thing, I guess, for this Government is to raise the bar and make some candidates disappear.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: I understand the Minister has said that the changes are not targeted at any individual, but I am sure the Minister would agree that the changes will narrow down the pool of eligible presidential candidates going forward.

sections.label: WP opposes Elected President
sections.summary: The WP does not see the need to have an Elected President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: The WP does not see the need to have an Elected President.

sections.label: Questions on reluctant candidates and race
sections.summary: The speaker asks about reluctant candidates, legitimacy of a sole candidate, and whether race and the Elected Presidency serve the Reserves or PAP control.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: How many reluctant candidates does this Government intend to field, just to give the electorate a semblance of contest, before we may end up with a reluctant President?

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: And if this Government wants to narrow down the field to a sole candidate, where is the legitimacy to real power?

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: Race has never been an issue for the highest office of our land until the Elected Presidency came along.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: Is the Elected Presidency the best platform to safeguard the Reserves or merely a veiled attempt by the PAP to safeguard its control over all levels of government at the same time?

sections.label: President's veto and Council advice
sections.summary: The speaker notes the amendment enlarges the President's veto powers and asks whether a Bill should return to Parliament if the President assents against Council advice.

sentences.speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In the proposed amendment to the Constitution, I note that the intention is to enlarge the President's veto powers, with the President acting on the advice of the Council.

sentences.speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: If the President exercises his veto vote contrary to the Council's advice, the Government may trigger the overruling mechanism, presumably because the President must take the advice of the Council seriously.

sentences.speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: However, should the President assent despite the Council recommending a veto, the Bill still becomes law.

sentences.speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Should not the same rationale apply and the Bill be then sent back to Parliament for further deliberation and debate?

sections.label: Support for minority Elected President
sections.summary: The speaker supports the amendment because it can strengthen society and mutual respect and tolerance among races.

sentences.speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Government announced that once the Constitutional amendment is passed, we will have an Elected President from the minorities from time to time.

sentences.speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I support this amendment because I believe this can further strengthen our society, as well as the mutual respect and tolerance among the different races.

sections.label: Hope for unity and minority support
sections.summary: The speaker hopes Chinese Singaporeans understand minority citizens, support a minority President, avoid stirring race and religion, and stay united as one people.

sentences.speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: We have all experienced that feeling – a not so nice feeling.

sentences.speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So I hope that as Chinese, we can understand the challenges, loneliness and aspirations of our minority fellow citizens; I hope that we can support our minority President; I hope that we will not use race and religion for our own self-interest to stir up problems; I hope that Singapore will always be one nation and one people; I hope we can always say that we are Singapore Citizens, regardless of race, language and religion, united as one.
